div.p: When, on my way home from Cilicia, I had come to Rhodes, and news was brought to me there of the death of Quintus Hortensius, I felt a grief greater than the common opinion would have looked for. For in losing a friend I saw myself deprived both of a pleasant companionship and of the bond of many mutual services; and I grieved that by the death of so distinguished an augur the prestige of our college was diminished. In this train of thought I recalled that he had co-opted me into the college, where under oath he had given his judgement of my worth, and that he had inaugurated me — so that by the established usage of the augurs I owed him the reverence due to a parent.

My distress was the greater because, in so great a dearth of wise and good citizens, this excellent man, bound to me as he was by partnership in all our counsels, had been taken from us at the most adverse season of the commonwealth, leaving us a bitter longing for his authority and good sense; and I grieved that I had lost not, as most supposed, a rival and a detractor of my own renown, but rather a companion and partner in a glorious labour.

For if, in the pursuit of the lighter arts, tradition records that famous poets have grieved at the death of poets who were their contemporaries, with what feelings ought I to have borne the death of one with whom it was more glorious to contend than to have no rival at all? — especially since not only was my course never hindered by him, nor his by me, but on the contrary each was always helped by the other, by sharing counsel, by warning, and by goodwill.

But since he, blessed with a kind of unbroken good fortune, departed from life at his own season rather than that of his fellow citizens, and died at the very time when, had he lived, he could more easily have mourned the commonwealth than aided it — and since he lived as long as it was permitted to live well and happily in the state — let us grieve, if grieve we must, over our own loss and disadvantage, but let us attend the timeliness of his death with goodwill rather than with pity, so that, whenever we think of so illustrious and fortunate a man, we may seem to love him rather than ourselves.

For if we grieve only because it is no longer granted us to enjoy his company, that is a misfortune of our own, which we should bear with moderation, lest we seem to refer it not to friendship but to our own private advantage; but if we are tormented as though some bitterness had befallen him himself, we interpret his supreme good fortune with too little gratitude.

For if Quintus Hortensius were still living, he might perhaps regret other things along with the rest of the good and brave citizens; but this grief he would feel beyond all others, or with few to share it, when he saw the forum of the Roman people — which had been, as it were, the theatre of his genius — despoiled and bereft of that learned voice, worthy of Roman and of Greek ears alike.

For my own part I am tormented in spirit that the commonwealth has need of the weapons of counsel, of talent, of authority — the very arts I had learned to handle, to which I had accustomed myself, and which belong both to a man of eminence in public life and to a well-ordered and well-constituted state. For if there was ever a time in the commonwealth when the authority and eloquence of a good citizen could wrench the weapons from the hands of angry fellow citizens, then surely it was when the advocacy of peace was shut out, whether by men's error or by their fear.

So it came about with me that, although there were far other things more to be mourned, yet I grieved at this: that at the very time when, having discharged the highest offices, my time of life ought to have taken refuge as in a harbour — not of idleness or sloth, but of moderate and honourable leisure — and when my own oratory had begun to grow grey and to attain a kind of ripeness and, as it were, old age, just then were those weapons taken up which even those who had learned to use them gloriously could not find how to use for the public safety.

And so it seems to me that those men lived fortunately and happily — in other states, but most of all in ours — to whom it was granted to enjoy at once the prestige and glory of great deeds and the praise of wisdom besides. The memory and recollection of these men was a genuine pleasure to me amid my greatest and gravest cares, when I lately came upon it in the course of a certain conversation.

For while I was walking in the colonnade and was at leisure at home, Marcus Brutus came to me, as was his custom, with Titus Pomponius — men so closely bound to each other, and so dear and delightful to me, that at the sight of them all the anxiety about the commonwealth that had been distressing me subsided. After I had greeted them, "Well," said I, "Brutus and Atticus, is there any news at last?" "None at all," said Brutus, "that you would care to hear, or that I would venture to assert for certain."

Then Atticus said, "We have come to you in such a mind that there should be silence about politics, and that we should rather hear something from you than burden you with any annoyance." "You, Atticus," I said, "both relieve me of care while you are present, and have given me great comfort while absent. For it was by your letter first that I was restored and recalled to my former studies." Then he said, "I read with great pleasure the letter that Brutus sent you from Asia, in which he seemed to me both to advise you wisely and to console you most affectionately."

"You judged rightly," I said; "for you must know that by that letter I was recalled, as if to behold the light, out of a long disorder of my whole well-being. And just as, after that disaster at Cannae, the Roman people first rose up again at the battle of Marcellus near Nola, and afterwards many prosperous events followed one upon another, so, after the gravest reverses of my own and the common fortunes, nothing befell me before the letter of Brutus that I could wish for, or that in any degree lightened my anxieties."

Then Brutus said, "I certainly wished to bring this about, and I reap a great reward, if indeed in so great a matter I have achieved what I intended. But I should like to know what it was in Atticus's letter that delighted you." "That letter, Brutus," I said, "brought me not only delight but, as I hope, salvation." "Salvation?" he said. "What sort of letter, then, was that so admirable one?" "Could there have been," I said, "any greeting more welcome to me, or more suited to this time, than that book of his by which he addressed me and roused me, as it were, when I lay prostrate?"

Then he said, "You mean, no doubt, the one in which he embraced briefly — and, as it seemed to me at least, with great care — the whole record of history?" "That very book, Brutus," I said, "I declare to have been my salvation." Then Atticus said, "Nothing could be more gratifying to me than what you say; but what, after all, did that book contain that could be either new to you or of so great use?"

"It held for me," I said, "many things that were indeed new, and the very usefulness I was seeking — that, with the sequences of the periods laid out, I might see everything at a single glance. And when I had begun to study it eagerly, the very handling of letters proved my salvation, and reminded me, Pomponius, that I should take from you yourself something for my own restoration, and to repay you with a gift that, if not equal, should yet be welcome — although that Hesiodic precept is praised by the learned, which bids us return by the same measure we have received, or even with more, if we can.

For my part I will surely render you full measure of goodwill, but I do not think I am yet able to render the thing itself; and I ask you to pardon me for this. For there is nothing from a new crop, as farmers have, out of which I might repay you what I received — so wholly is every yield checked, and the flower of my old abundance withered and scorched by drought — nor from anything stored away, which lies in darkness and to which all access is blocked for me, though it was once open to me almost alone. So I shall sow something, as it were, in untilled and abandoned soil; and this I shall cultivate so carefully that I may be able even by my pains to increase the bounty of your gift — if only my mind can do what the field can, which, when it has lain fallow for many years, is wont to bring forth more abundant crops." Then he said,

"For my part I shall both await what you promise, and I shall not exact it save at your convenience; and it will be most welcome to me if you discharge the debt." "I too," said Brutus, "must await what you promise to Atticus, although perhaps I, the voluntary agent of his interest, shall demand from you what he himself, to whom you owe it, says he will not exact to your inconvenience."

"But I, Brutus," I said, "will not pay you, unless I first take security from you that no one else, with a claim, shall make demand on that account." "By Hercules," he said, "I would not venture to make you that promise. For this man here, who declines, I can see will be a creditor not, indeed, troublesome to you, but persistent and keen for all that." Then Pomponius said, "For my part, I think Brutus is telling no lie. For I think I shall now venture to dun you, since after a long interval I have just now noticed you a little more cheerful.

And so, since this man has declared that he will exact what is owed to me, I demand of you on his behalf what you owe to him." "And what is that?" I said. "That you write something," he said; "for your pen has long been silent. For since you published those books on the commonwealth, we have certainly received nothing from you afterwards — and it was by these that we ourselves were spurred and kindled to set down a record of our own history. But those works whenever you can; and that you may be able, I beg.

But now," he said, "if your mind is free, set forth for us what we ask." "And what is that?" I said. "What you lately laid out for us at your place at Tusculum, about the orators — when they began to be, and who they were, and of what quality. When I had reported this conversation to your Brutus, or rather our Brutus, he said he was most eager to hear it. And so we have chosen this day, since we knew you to be free. Therefore, if it is convenient for you, set forth for Brutus and me what you had begun."

"For my part," I said, "if I can, I will satisfy you." "You can," he said: "only relax your mind a little, or indeed, if you can, set it free." "It was here, then, Pomponius, that the conversation took its start — from my mentioning that I had heard the cause of Deiotarus, that most loyal and excellent king, defended by Brutus most elegantly and most fully." "I know," he said, "that the conversation was drawn from that beginning, and that you, lamenting Brutus's lot, bewailed, as it were, the desolation of the courts and of the forum." "I did indeed do that," I said, "and I often do it.

For often, Brutus, as I look at you, it comes into my mind to fear what course your admirable nature, your exquisite learning, and your singular industry will at last be allowed to run. For when you had been engaged in the greatest cases, and when my generation was already yielding to you and lowering its fasces, suddenly in the state, when other things fell, that very eloquence too, of which we are beginning to speak, fell silent."

Then he said, "For other reasons I both grieve at this and think it ought to be grieved over; but in speaking it is not so much its fruit and glory that delights me as the pursuit itself and the practice of it — and that nothing shall snatch from me, especially with you so devoted to me. For no one can speak well unless he understands wisely; and therefore whoever gives his pains to true eloquence gives them to wisdom, of which not even in the greatest wars can anyone be deprived without distress."

"Admirably, Brutus," I said, "do you speak; and I am the more delighted by that praise of eloquence because the other things that were once held in the highest esteem in this state, there is no one so lowly as not to think either that he can attain them or that he has attained them; whereas I see no one made eloquent by victory. But, that the conversation may unfold more easily, let us conduct it sitting, if you please." And when the same had pleased them, we sat down in a little meadow beside the statue of Plato.

Here I began: "To praise eloquence, and to set forth how great is its power and how great the dignity it confers on those who have attained it — this is neither our purpose in this place nor necessary. But this I would affirm without any hesitation: that whether it is begotten by some art, or by practice, or by nature, it is the most difficult thing in the world. For of the five elements of which it is said to consist, each single one is in itself a great art. From this it can be estimated how great a power, and how great a difficulty, the concurrence of these five greatest arts must have.

Greece is my witness, which, though it was fired with zeal for eloquence and has long excelled and surpassed all others in it, yet possesses all its other arts older — and not only discovered but even brought to perfection long before this developed power and copiousness of speech. When I look upon it, Atticus, your Athens above all comes to my mind and shines out, as it were — the city in which an orator first stood forth, and in which oratory first began to be entrusted to records and to writing.

Yet before Pericles, of whom certain writings are preserved, and Thucydides — who lived not when Athens was being born but when it was already grown — there is no piece of writing that has any ornament and seems to be the work of an orator. And yet there is an opinion that Pisistratus, who lived many years before these, and Solon, somewhat older still, and afterwards Clisthenes, were men of much power in speaking, as far as those times allowed.

Some years after this age, as can be discerned from the records of Attica, came Themistocles, who is agreed to have excelled both in prudence and in eloquence; after him Pericles, who, though he flourished in every kind of excellence, was yet most renowned for this distinction. Cleon too, in those times, is agreed to have been a turbulent citizen indeed, but eloquent for all that.

Nearly of this age were Alcibiades, Critias, and Theramenes; and what kind of oratory flourished in those times can best be understood from the writings of Thucydides, who himself lived then. They were grand in their words, thick with maxims, brief by their compression of matter, and for that very reason at times somewhat obscure.

But as soon as it was understood how great a power a carefully wrought and, in a manner, composed oratory had, then too many teachers of speaking suddenly arose. Then Gorgias of Leontini, Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Protagoras of Abdera, Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis were held in great honour; and many others in those same times professed to teach — in words arrogant enough, to be sure — how the weaker cause, for so they spoke, could be made the stronger by speaking.

Against these set himself Socrates, who by a certain subtlety of argument was wont to refute their teachings. Out of his most copious conversations there came forth men of the highest learning; and then for the first time philosophy is said to have been discovered — not that earlier philosophy of nature, but this in which there is debate about things good and bad and about the life and morals of men. But since this kind of subject is foreign to what we have proposed, let us put off the philosophers to another time, and return to the orators from whom we digressed.

There arose, then, when those old men I mentioned a little before were already aged, Isocrates, whose house stood open like a school and a workshop of eloquence to all Greece — a great orator and a perfect teacher, though he lacked the light of the forum and within his walls nourished that glory which, in my judgement at least, no one afterwards attained. He both wrote much himself most admirably and taught others; and besides surpassing his predecessors in other respects, he was the first to understand that even in prose, while you avoid verse, a certain measure and rhythm must nevertheless be preserved.

For before him there was no such structure of words, as it were, and no rounding-off to a rhythm; or if there ever was, it was not apparent that it had been deliberately sought — which is perhaps a merit, but still it came about then more by nature and by chance, never by any method or any observation of rule.

For nature herself, by a certain rounding of the words, comprehends and closes the thought; and when this is bound up in fitting words, it usually falls into rhythm as well. For the ears themselves judge what is full and what is empty, and the breath, as if by a kind of necessity, sets a limit to the grouping of the words; and in this it is disgraceful not only to fall short but even to labour.

Then came Lysias — himself, indeed, not engaged in cases before the courts, but an eminently subtle and elegant writer, whom one might now almost venture to call a perfect orator. For one might easily call Demosthenes plainly perfect, a man in whom nothing whatever is lacking. Nothing acute could be devised in the cases that Lysias wrote, nothing, so to speak, cunning, nothing artful, that the other did not see; nothing could be said with subtlety, nothing closely, nothing clearly, by which anything could be made more polished; nothing, on the other hand, grand, nothing impetuous, nothing adorned either with weight of words or of thought, by which anything could be made more sublime.

Next to him came Hyperides and Aeschines and Lycurgus and Dinarchus and the man of whom no writings survive, Demades, and many others besides. For this age poured forth this abundance; and, as my opinion holds, that uncorrupted sap and blood of the orators lasted down to this age, in which there was a natural, not a painted, brilliance.

For Demetrius of Phalerum succeeded those old men — a young man, the most learned indeed of all of them, but trained not so much in the arms as in the wrestling-school. And so he delighted the Athenians more than he inflamed them. For he had come forth into the sun and dust, not as from a soldier's tent, but as from the shaded retreats of Theophrastus, that most learned man.

He was the first to bend oratory and to render it soft and tender, and chose to seem agreeable, as he was, rather than weighty — but with that sweetness by which he might suffuse men's minds, not break through them, and only so far as to leave behind a memory of his own neatness, not, as Eupolis wrote of Pericles, to leave together with delight a sting also in the minds of those who had heard him.

Do you see, then, even in that very city in which eloquence was both born and reared, how late it came forth into the light? — since before the age of Solon and Pisistratus there is no record of anyone as an able speaker. And these men, indeed, by the reckoning of the Roman people's age, are old; but by the reckoning of the generations of the Athenians they ought to seem young. For although they flourished in the reign of Servius Tullius, yet Athens had already existed much longer than Rome has to the present day. Yet I do not doubt that oratory always had great power.

For Homer would not in Trojan times have assigned so much praise in speaking to Ulysses and to Nestor — the one of whom he wished to have force, the other sweetness — had the honour of eloquence not already existed even then; nor would the poet himself have been so ornate in speech and so plainly an orator. And although his dates are uncertain, yet he lived many years before Romulus, if indeed he was not later than the elder Lycurgus, by whom the discipline of the Lacedaemonians was bound fast with laws.

But a zeal for this kind, and a greater power, is recognized in Pisistratus. Finally, in the next age, Themistocles followed him — by our reckoning very ancient, but by that of the Athenians not really so old. For he lived when Greece was already under kings, but our state was not so long since freed from the rule of kings. For that gravest war of the Volscians, in which Coriolanus took part as an exile, fell at almost the same time as the war with the Persians, and the fortune of those famous men was alike;

for each, when he had been an excellent citizen, was driven out by the injustice of an ungrateful people, betook himself to the enemy, and quieted the impulse of his anger by death. For although you have it otherwise about Coriolanus, Atticus, grant me nevertheless that I may agree rather with this manner of death." But he, with a laugh, said: "As you please, indeed; since rhetoricians are permitted to invent in their histories, that they may have something to say more pointedly. For just as you now do about Coriolanus, so Clitarchus, so Stratocles, invented about Themistocles.

For the man whom Thucydides — who was an Athenian, of the highest birth and a man of the highest rank, and a little later in time — wrote to have died merely of disease and to have been secretly buried in Attica, adding that there was a suspicion that he had brought death upon himself by poison: this man, these others say, when he had sacrificed a bull, caught the blood in a bowl, and, having drunk it, fell down dead. For this death they could adorn rhetorically and tragically, while that common death offered no material for ornament. Therefore, since it suits you that everything in Themistocles was matched with Coriolanus, you may take the bowl from me too; I will even provide the victim, that Coriolanus may be plainly a second Themistocles."

"Let it be," I said, "as you please, about that; and I shall hereafter touch history more cautiously when you are listening — you whom I can praise as a most scrupulous authority on Roman affairs. But it was about then that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, of whom I spoke before, first brought learning to bear; and although there was then no rhetorical art, yet, trained by the natural philosopher Anaxagoras, he had readily transferred the exercise of his mind from recondite and abstruse matters to causes of the forum and of the people. By his sweetness Athens was most delighted, his richness and copiousness it admired, and the force and terror of the same man's speaking it feared.

This age, then, first produced at Athens an almost perfect orator. For neither among those founding a commonwealth, nor among those waging wars, nor among the embarrassed and those bound fast by the domination of kings, does the desire for speaking usually arise. Eloquence is the companion of peace and the comrade of leisure, and, as it were, a nursling of a state already well constituted.

And so Aristotle says that when, the tyrants having been overthrown in Sicily, private property was after a long interval reclaimed through the courts, then for the first time — since that people was keen and contentious by nature — the Sicilians Corax and Tisias composed an art and precepts; for before that no one had been wont to speak by method or by art, though most spoke carefully and in due order; and that disputations on illustrious subjects, which are now called commonplaces, had been written and made ready by Protagoras;

that Gorgias did the same — who, he says, composed praises and censures of particular things, because he judged it most especially the orator's task to be able to amplify a thing by praise and again to bring it low by censure; that Antiphon of Rhamnus had certain similar things written, than whom no one ever pleaded a capital cause better, when he defended himself — so the wealthy authority Thucydides wrote, who heard it;

for Lysias was at first wont to profess that there was an art of speaking; then, because Theodorus was subtler in the art but rather meagre in actual speeches, Lysias began to write speeches for others and laid the art aside; and similarly Isocrates at first denied that there was an art of speaking, but was wont to write speeches for others to use in the courts; but since on that account, because he was, as it were, breaking the law against 'circumventing anyone by a judgement,' he was himself often summoned into court, he ceased to write speeches for others and transferred himself wholly to composing arts.

And these, then, are the birth and the springs of the Greek orators that you see — old by the reckoning of our annals, but, by their own, recent enough. For before the Athenian state was charmed with this glory of speaking, it had already accomplished many memorable things both in domestic and in military affairs. But this pursuit was not common to all Greece; it was peculiar to Athens.

For who knows of an Argive or a Corinthian or a Theban orator in those times? — unless one cares to make some surmise about Epaminondas, a learned man. But of a Lacedaemonian I have heard that, down to this present time, there was not one. Menelaus himself Homer represents as agreeable indeed, but speaking few words. Now brevity is at times a merit in some part of speaking, but in eloquence taken as a whole it has no merit.

But outside Greece there were great pursuits of speaking, and the highest honours paid to this distinction made the name of orators illustrious. For as soon as eloquence had once been carried out from the Piraeus, it traversed all the islands and so wandered over the whole of Asia that it smeared itself with foreign manners and lost all that wholesomeness and, as it were, soundness of Attic diction, and almost unlearned how to speak. Hence the Asiatic orators, not to be despised indeed either for swiftness or for copiousness, but too little compressed and too redundant; the Rhodians sounder and more like the Athenians.

But enough of the Greeks; and indeed these very matters were perhaps not necessary." Then Brutus said, "How necessary they were I could not easily say; but they were certainly pleasant to me, and not only not long but even shorter than I could have wished." "Very well," I said; "but let us come to our own countrymen, about whom it is hard to understand more than what one may surmise from the records.

For who would think that quickness of mind was wanting to Lucius Brutus, that famous founder of your nobility? — who from the oracle of Apollo so acutely and cleverly drew an inference about kissing his mother; who veiled the highest prudence under a pretence of folly; who expelled a most powerful king, the son of a most illustrious king, and bound the state, freed from perpetual domination, with annual magistracies, with laws, and with courts; who deprived his own colleague of his office, that he might remove from the state the very memory of the royal name — a thing that certainly could not have been brought about had it not been accomplished by persuasion in speech.

We see likewise that a few years after the kings were driven out, when the commons had encamped near the bank of the Anio at the third milestone and had occupied that hill which was called the Sacred, Marcus Valerius as dictator quieted the discord by speaking, and that for this reason the highest honours were paid to him, and that he was the first, for that very reason, to be called Maximus. Nor do I think that even Lucius Valerius Potitus could do nothing by speaking — he who, after the hatred against the decemvirs, soothed by his laws and his harangues the commons who had been roused against the senators.

We may surmise that Appius Claudius was eloquent, since he recalled the senate, when it was just now inclined toward peace with Pyrrhus; we may surmise it of Gaius Fabricius, since he was sent as an envoy to Pyrrhus about recovering the captives; of Tiberius Coruncanius, because from the commentaries of the pontiffs he seems to have been by far the most powerful in talent; of Manius Curius, because, as tribune of the commons, when Appius the Blind as interrex, an eloquent man, was holding the elections contrary to the laws, and would not accept a consul from the commons, Curius compelled the senators first to give their sanction — which was a very great thing, since the Maenian law had not yet been passed.

We may surmise something too about the talent of Marcus Popilius, who, when he was consul and was at the same time performing a public sacrifice in his cloak, since he was flamen of Carmenta, on news being brought of a stirring-up and sedition of the commons against the senators, came just as he was, wrapped in his cloak, into the assembly, and quieted the sedition by his authority and by his speaking. But that these men were held to be orators, or that there was then any reward of eloquence at all, I do not think I have read anywhere; I am led only by conjecture to surmise it.

Gaius Flaminius too is said — he who as tribune of the commons carried the law for distributing the Gallic and Picene land man by man, and who as consul was killed at Trasimene — to have had power with the people by speaking. Quintus Maximus Verrucosus also was held an orator in those times, and Quintus Metellus, he who in the Second Punic War was consul with Lucius Veturius Philo. But the first of whom it is on record, and of whom it is handed down that he was eloquent and was so held, is Marcus Cornelius Cethegus, for whose eloquence the authority is — and, in my judgement, a competent one — Quintus Ennius, especially since he both heard him himself and writes of him when dead: from which there is no suspicion that he lied for friendship's sake.
The passage is, then, as I think, thus in the ninth book of his Annals:
To these is added an orator, Cornelius, sweet of speech, Cethegus Marcus, colleague of Tuditanus, Marcus's son —

he both calls him an orator and ascribes to him sweetness of speech, which now indeed is not so common in most men — for some orators now bark rather than speak — but is surely the greatest praise of eloquence —
he was called by those of his countrymen of old, the men who then were living and passing their time, the chosen flower of the people —
aptly, indeed;
for as a man's glory is his talent, so the very light of talent is eloquence, in which those men of old admirably said that the excellent man was the flower of the people —
and the marrow of Persuasion.

Persuasion, whom the Greeks call Peitho, of which the orator is the maker — this Ennius called Suada; and he means that Cethegus was its marrow, so that the goddess whom Eupolis wrote to have sat upon the lips of Pericles, of her this orator of ours was, he said, the marrow.

But this Cethegus was consul with Publius Tuditanus in the Second Punic War, and Marcus Cato was quaestor under these consuls, just a hundred and forty years before I was consul; and unless this very fact had been known by the single testimony of Ennius, antiquity, as it has overwhelmed perhaps many others, would have overwhelmed him too in oblivion. And what the speech of that age was can be understood from the writings of Naevius. For under these consuls, as it is written in the old commentaries, Naevius died — although our Varro, a most diligent investigator of antiquity, thinks there is an error here, and prolongs the life of Naevius further. For Plautus died under the consuls Publius Claudius and Lucius Porcius, twenty years after those I mentioned before, when Cato was censor.

This Cethegus, then, Cato followed in age, who was consul nine years after him. Him we reckon a very ancient man — he who died under the consuls Lucius Marcius and Manius Manilius, just eighty-six years before I was consul. Nor indeed have I any one older whose writings I think worth bringing forward, unless this very speech of Appius the Blind about Pyrrhus, and certain eulogies of the dead, chance to please someone.

And by Hercules these at least survive: for the families themselves preserved them as their ornaments and memorials, both for use, if someone of the same line should die, and for the memory of their family's praises, and to illustrate their own nobility. And yet by these eulogies the history of our affairs has been made more faulty. For many things are written in them which were never done: false triumphs, too many consulships, false pedigrees too, and transitions to the commons, when men of humbler station were poured into another family of the same name — as if I were to say that I was descended from that Manius Tullius who, a patrician, was consul with Servius Sulpicius in the tenth year after the kings were expelled.

But the speeches of Cato are well-nigh as many as those of the Attic Lysias — of whom I think there are very many; for he is Attic, since he was certainly both born and died at Athens and discharged every office of a citizen, although Timaeus reclaims him for Syracuse, as if under the Licinian and Mucian law — and there is in a certain way some likeness even between them. They are acute, elegant, witty, brief; but the Greek is more fortunate in every kind of praise. For he has his devoted admirers, who pursue not so much the plump build of body as the slender forms, and whom, provided only the health is good, the very leanness delights — although in Lysias there are often even sinews, so that nothing could be more vigorous; but he is certainly, in his whole kind, more spare — yet still he has his own admirers, who take great pleasure in this very subtlety of his.

But which of our orators — those, at least, who now exist — reads Cato? Or who knows him at all? And yet what a man, good gods! I pass over the citizen, the senator, the general; for it is the orator we are seeking in this place: who was weightier than he in praising? more biting in censure? more pointed in his maxims? subtler in instructing and expounding? His speeches, more than a hundred and fifty of them — those at least that I have so far found and read — are crammed with brilliant words and matter. Let them choose from these the things worthy of note and praise: all the virtues of an orator will be found in them.

And his Origins, again — what flower or what light of eloquence do they not possess? He lacks admirers, just as for many ages already did Philistus of Syracuse and Thucydides himself. For as Theopompus, by the loftiness and elevation of his style, eclipses the clipped maxims of these men — at times too not sufficiently clear, both for their brevity and their excessive pointedness — the same that Demosthenes does to Lysias, so this style of later men, heaped up, as it were, to a greater height, has blocked the lights of Cato.

But there is this ignorance in our countrymen, that these very men who in the Greeks are delighted with antiquity and with that subtlety which they call Attic, do not even know it in Cato. They wish to be like Hyperides and Lysias. I commend them.

But why are they not willing to be like the Catos? They say they delight in the Attic kind of speaking. Wisely, indeed; and would that they imitated it — not the bones only but the blood as well! Yet it is welcome, what they wish. — Why, then, are Lysias and Hyperides loved, while Cato is utterly ignored? His speech is more ancient and some of his words are rather rough. For so they spoke in those days. Change that, which then he could not, and add rhythm, and that the speech may be better knit, arrange and, as it were, cement the very words — which not even the old Greeks practised — and now you will set no one before Cato.

The Greeks think that oratory is adorned if they use those substitutions of words which they call tropes, and those figures of thought and of speech which they call schemata: it is hardly credible how frequent and how distinct Cato is in both kinds. Nor indeed am I unaware that this orator is not yet sufficiently polished, and that something more perfect must be sought; for he is so old by the reckoning of our times that no one's writing survives, worth reading at least, that is older. But in all the arts antiquity is treated with greater honour than in this one art of speaking alone. For who among those who notice these lesser matters does not understand that the statues of Canachus are too stiff to imitate the truth; that those of Calamis, hard indeed, are yet softer than those of Canachus; that those of Myron are not yet sufficiently brought to the truth, yet such as you would not hesitate to call beautiful; and those of Polyclitus more beautiful still and now plainly perfect, as they are wont to seem to me at least? The case in painting is similar; in which we praise the forms and outlines of Zeuxis and Polygnotus and Timanthes and of those who used no more than four colours; but in Aetion, Nicomachus, Protogenes, Apelles, all is now perfect. And I am inclined to think the same happens in all other things too: for nothing is at once both discovered and perfected. Nor ought it to be doubted that there were poets before Homer, as can be understood from those songs which in his work are sung both at the feasts of the Phaeacians and at those of the suitors. And our old verses, where are they? —
which once the Fauns and seers used to sing,
when neither the crags of the Muses . . .
nor was anyone studious of learned words before this man —

so he says of himself, and does not lie in his boasting: for so the matter stands. For both the Latin Odyssey is, as it were, some work of Daedalus, and the plays of Livius are not quite worthy to be read a second time.

And yet this Livius first produced a play in the consulship of Gaius Claudius, son of Caecus, and Marcus Tuditanus, in the very year before Ennius was born, and in the five hundred and fourteenth year after the founding of Rome — so says the man whom we follow. For there is a dispute among writers about the number of the years. Accius, however, wrote that Livius was taken prisoner at Tarentum by Quintus Maximus, in his fifth consulship, thirty years after Livius had produced a play (so both Atticus writes and we have found in the old commentaries),

and that he produced a play eleven years later, in the consulship of Gaius Cornelius and Quintus Minucius, at the games of Iuventas which Salinator had vowed at the battle of Sena. In which Accius's error was so great that under these consuls Ennius was forty years old: and if Livius were his contemporary, then he who first gave a play was somewhat younger than those who had produced many plays before these consuls — both Plautus and Naevius.

If these matters seem less fitted to this conversation, Brutus, lay it to Atticus, who fired me with a zeal for tracing the ages and times of illustrious men." "For my part," said Brutus, "I both take delight in that marking-out, as it were, of the periods, and, with a view to the task you have undertaken — to distinguish the kinds of orators by their ages — I think that diligence of yours well suited to it."

"Rightly, Brutus," I said, "do you understand it. And would that there survived those songs which, many ages before his own time, Cato left written in his Origins to have been sung at feasts by individual banqueters about the praises of famous men! Yet the Punic War of that poet whom Ennius reckons among the seers and Fauns delights us, like a work of Myron.

Let Ennius, to be sure, be more perfect, as he certainly is; yet if he despised that other poet, as he pretends, he would not, in pursuing all the wars, have left out that first Punic War, the fiercest of all. But he himself tells why he does so. "Others," he says, "have written the matter in verse" — and they wrote it brilliantly indeed, even if less polished than you. Nor in truth ought it to seem otherwise to you, who either took much from Naevius, if you admit it, or, if you deny it, stole it.

Older in years than this Cato were Gaius Flaminius, Gaius Varro, Quintus Maximus, Quintus Metellus, Publius Lentulus, and Publius Crassus, who was consul with the elder Africanus. Scipio himself, we are told, was not without speech. His son indeed — he who adopted this younger Scipio from Paullus — had he been sound in body, would have been reckoned among the foremost in eloquence; this is shown both by some little speeches and by a certain history written in Greek most sweetly.

Of the same number was Sextus Aelius, the most learned of all in civil law, but ready in speaking too. And among the younger men, Gaius Sulpicius Gallus, who of all the nobility most studied Greek letters; he too was held among the orators and was in other respects polished and elegant. For there was now a smoother and more brilliant fashion of speaking. For while he as praetor was holding the games of Apollo, and had produced the play Thyestes, Ennius met his death, in the consulship of Quintus Marcius and Gnaeus Servilius.

There lived in the same times Tiberius Gracchus, son of Publius, who was twice consul and censor, and whose speech in Greek among the Rhodians survives; a citizen who is agreed to have been both weighty and eloquent. They say too that Publius Scipio Nasica, who was called Corculum, who likewise was twice consul and censor, was held eloquent — the son of that Scipio who received the sacred objects; they mention also Lucius Lentulus, who was consul with Gaius Figulus; Quintus Nobilior, son of Marcus, now by his father's example devoted to the study of letters — who even gave Roman citizenship to Quintus Ennius, who had served with his father in Aetolia, when he as one of three commissioners had led out a colony — and Titus Annius Luscus, the colleague of this Quintus Fulvius, they say was not without speech;

and indeed Lucius Paullus, the father of Africanus, easily maintained the part of a leading citizen by his speaking. And in truth even then, while Cato was still living — who departed from life at the age of eighty-five, when in that very year he had spoken against Servius Galba before the people with the utmost vehemence, which speech too he left in writing —

but while Cato was living, many younger orators flourished at one time. For both Aulus Albinus, he who wrote a history in Greek, who was consul with Lucius Lucullus, was both lettered and eloquent; and together with him a certain place was held also by Servius Fulvius, and with them Servius Fabius Pictor, well versed both in law and in letters and in antiquity; and Quintus Fabius Labeo was adorned with nearly the same praises. For Quintus Metellus, he whose four sons were of consular rank, was held among the foremost in eloquence — he who spoke for Lucius Cotta when Africanus was the accuser; of him there are both other speeches and one against Tiberius Gracchus, set out in the annals of Gaius Fannius.

Then Lucius Cotta himself was held an old hand; — but Gaius Laelius and Publius Africanus were among the foremost in eloquence, whose speeches survive, from which a judgement can be formed of the orators' talents. But among these, going a little before them in age, Servius Galba without dispute excelled in eloquence; and doubtless he was the first among the Latins to handle those works proper and, as it were, lawful to orators: to digress from his theme for the sake of ornament, to delight the mind, to move it, to amplify a matter, to use appeals to pity and commonplaces. But somehow the speeches of this man, who is agreed to have excelled in eloquence, are rather meagre and smell more of antiquity than do those of Laelius or Scipio or even Cato himself; and so they have withered away, so that now they scarcely appear.

As for the talent of Laelius and Scipio themselves, although the reputation is such that very much is ascribed to both, yet the praise for speaking is more brilliant in Laelius. And yet the speech of Laelius on the colleges is not better than any you please of Scipio's many; not that there is anything sweeter than that of Laelius, or that anything could be said more solemnly about religion, but Laelius is nevertheless much more antique and rough than Scipio; and, since in speaking tastes differ, Laelius seems to me to take more delight in antiquity and gladly to use words too a little more old-fashioned.

But it is the way of men to be unwilling that the same person should excel in several things. For as in military glory no one can aspire to rival Africanus — in which very thing we find that Laelius was distinguished in the war against Viriathus — so in talent, in letters, in eloquence, and finally in wisdom, although they grant the first rank to both, they gladly assign the precedence to Laelius. And it seems to me to have been so awarded not only by the judgement of others, but also by their own concession between themselves.

There was indeed then a custom, as better in other respects, so in this very thing more humane, that men were ready in assigning to each his own. I remember that at Smyrna I heard from Publius Rutilius Rufus, when he said that it had befallen him as a young man that, by a decree of the senate, Publius Scipio and Decimus Brutus, I think, as consuls were holding an inquiry into a great and atrocious matter. For when a slaughter had been committed in the Silan forest, and well-known men killed, and the household was accused — and in part also the freemen of that company which had farmed the pitch-works under the censors Publius Cornelius and Lucius Mummius — the senate decreed that the consuls should inquire into and decide that matter.

Laelius pleaded the cause for the tax-farmers carefully, as he was always wont, and elegantly. When the consuls, having heard the case, had pronounced a 'further hearing' by the advice of their council, after a few days had passed Laelius spoke again, much more carefully and better, and again in the same way the matter was postponed by the consuls. Then Laelius, when the company had escorted him home and given him thanks and begged him not to wear himself out, spoke thus: that what he had done he had done zealously and carefully for their honour's sake, but that he thought that case could be defended more weightily and more vehemently by Servius Galba, because he was more vigorous and keen in speaking. And so on the advice

of Gaius Laelius the tax-farmers brought the case to Galba; but he, because he had to succeed such a man, undertook it modestly and hesitantly. There was one whole intervening day, as in an adjournment, which Galba spent entirely in considering and composing the case; and when the day of the hearing came, and Rutilius himself, at the company's request, had come early in the morning to Galba's house, to remind him and to bring him to the time of speaking, that man, until it was announced to him that the consuls had come down, with everyone shut out, was rehearsing in a certain vaulted room with educated slaves, to whom he was wont to dictate, one this, another that, at the same time. Meanwhile, when it was announced to him that it was time, he came out into the house with such a colour and such eyes that you would have thought he had pleaded the cause, not rehearsed it.

He added too — and he thought this to the purpose — that those secretaries came out badly mauled with Galba; from which he signified that the man had been vehement and fired not only in pleading but also in rehearsing. In short: with great expectation, before very many listeners, in the presence of Laelius himself, Galba pleaded that case with such force and such weight that scarcely any part of the speech was passed over in silence. And so, with many complaints and much appeal to pity employed, the company was freed from the inquiry that day, with everyone's approval.

From this narrative of Rutilius one may surmise that, since there are two chief merits in an orator — one of arguing subtly to instruct, the other of pleading weightily to move the minds of the hearers, and since he who inflames the judge accomplishes far more than he who instructs — there was elegance in Laelius, force in Galba. And this force was most especially recognized when, the Lusitanians having been killed by Servius Galba as praetor against the faith pledged, as it was thought, and when Lucius Libo as tribune of the commons was rousing the people and bringing a bill against Galba resembling a personal enactment, Marcus Cato, in extreme old age, as I said before, said much against Galba in advocating the law; which speech he entered in his Origins, a few days, or months, before he died.

Then Galba, refusing nothing on his own behalf and imploring the good faith of the Roman people, weeping, commended both his own children and the son also of Gaius Gallus, whose orphaned state and weeping was wonderfully pitiable on account of the recent memory of his most illustrious father; and he then snatched himself from the flames, the pity of the people having been stirred on account of the children, as the same Cato has left in writing. And I see too that Libo himself was not without speech, as can be understood from his orations.

When I had said this and had paused a little, "What then," said Brutus, "is the reason, if there was so great a virtue in Galba as an orator, that none of it appears in his speeches? — which I cannot wonder at in those who left nothing at all in writing." "For it is not the same reason, Brutus," I said, "for not writing and for not writing so well as men spoke. For we see that some orators, out of laziness, wrote nothing, lest a labour at home should be added to that of the forum — for most speeches are written down after being delivered, not in order to be delivered —; that others do not trouble to become better —

for nothing so much advances speaking as writing —; and that they do not desire a memorial of their talent for posterity, since they think they have attained a sufficiently great glory in speaking, and that it will seem even greater if their writings do not come before the judgement of critics; that others write nothing because they think they can speak better than they can write — which usually happens to men of very great talent but not sufficiently learned, as it did to Galba himself.

Galba, perhaps, the force not only of his talent but also of his spirit, and a certain natural feeling, kindled as he spoke and made his oratory both impetuous and weighty and vehement; but then, when at leisure he had taken up the pen, and all the movements of his spirit had failed the man like a wind, his oratory grew flabby. This is not wont to happen to those who pursue a more polished kind of speaking, because prudence never fails the orator, by using which he can speak and write in the same way; but the fire of the spirit is not always present, and when it has subsided, all that force and, as it were, flame of the orator is extinguished.
For this reason, then, the mind of Laelius seems to breathe even in his writings, but the force of Galba to have died.

There were too in the number of middling orators the brothers Lucius and Spurius Mummius, whose speeches both survive; Lucius indeed plain and antique, Spurius no more ornate, but yet more compact; for he was learned in the school of the Stoics. There are many speeches of Spurius Albinus. There are also those of Lucius and Gaius Aurelius Orestes, whom I see to have been counted in some number among the orators. Publius too

Popilius was both a distinguished citizen and not without speech; but Gaius his son was a fluent speaker; and Gaius Tuditanus, refined and polished in his whole life and manner of living, had also a kind of style of oratory accounted elegant. And in the same kind was reckoned Marcus Octavius, he who, having received an injury, broke Tiberius Gracchus by his patience — a citizen most steadfast in the best causes. But indeed Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, who was called Porcina, of nearly the same times as Galba, but a little younger, was both held a supreme orator and was, as appears from his speeches, a tolerably good writer.

In this Latin orator first there seem to me to have appeared both that smoothness of the Greeks and the rounding-off of words and a now, so to speak, artful pen. Two most talented young men, almost of an age, were wont eagerly to hear him, Gaius Carbo and Tiberius Gracchus; of whom there will now be a place to speak, when I have said a few words about the older men. For Quintus Pompeius was no contemptible orator in those times — a man who attained the highest offices, known by himself, without any recommendation from his ancestors.

Then Lucius Cassius had great power, not by eloquence, but by speaking nevertheless; a man popular not by liberality, as others were, but by his very grimness and severity; and to his ballot-law Marcus Antius Briso, tribune of the commons, long held out, with the support of the consul Marcus Lepidus; and that matter was a reproach to Publius Africanus, because it was thought that Briso had been led away from his opinion by his authority. Then the two Caepiones much supported their clients by counsel and tongue, but more by authority and influence. There are writings of Sextus Pompeius, not too thin, although like those of the ancients, and full of good sense. Publius Crassus

we are told was a much-approved orator at nearly the same times — one who was both strong in talent and in zeal, and had also certain teachings at home. For he had bound himself by marriage-tie to that supreme orator Servius Galba, to whose son Gaius he had given his daughter; and since he was the son of Publius Mucius and had a brother, Publius Scaevola, he had learned the civil law at home. In him it is agreed there was the highest industry and the greatest influence, since he was both consulted very much and pleaded.

To the ages of these were added the two Gaius Fannii, sons of Gaius and of Marcus; of whom the son of Gaius, who was consul with Domitius, left one speech on the allies and the Latin name against Gaius Gracchus, both a good and a noble one. Then Atticus said, "What then? Is that speech really Fannius's? For there was a varied opinion when we were boys. Some said it was written by Gaius Persius, a lettered man — the one whom Lucilius signifies to have been very learned; others, that many nobles, each what he could, contributed to that speech."

Then I said, "I have indeed heard those things from my elders, but I was never brought to believe them; and I believe that suspicion arose for this reason — because Fannius was held among the middling orators, while the speech was even the best of all the speeches of that time. But it is not of such a kind as to seem put together by several — for there is one tone of the whole speech and the same style —; nor would Gracchus have kept silent about Persius, when Fannius had reproached him about Menelaus of Marathus and the rest; especially since Fannius was never held tongueless. For he both pleaded causes regularly, and his tribunate, conducted by the judgement and authority of Publius Africanus, was not obscure. But the other Gaius Fannius, son of Marcus, son-in-law of Gaius Laelius, was harsher both in character and in his very manner of speaking.

By the instruction of his father-in-law — whom, because he had not been co-opted into the college of augurs, he did not much love, especially since Laelius had preferred to him as son-in-law the younger Quintus Scaevola (to whom, however, Laelius, excusing himself, said that he had given that not to the younger son-in-law but to the elder daughter) — yet by Laelius's instruction he had heard Panaetius. His whole faculty in speaking can be discerned from his own history, written not inelegantly, which is neither too inarticulate nor perfectly eloquent.

Mucius the augur, what was needed for himself, he himself spoke — as concerning extortion against Titus Albucius. He was not in the number of the orators; he excelled in the knowledge of civil law and in every kind of prudence. Lucius Caelius Antipater the writer was, as you see, brilliant for those times, very skilled in law, and the teacher of many, such as Lucius Crassus.

Would that in Tiberius Gracchus and Gaius Carbo there had been such a mind for governing the commonwealth well as there was talent for speaking well: assuredly no one would have surpassed these men in glory. But of them the one, on account of his most turbulent tribunate — to which, angered at the good men through the odium of the Numantine treaty, he had come — was killed by the commonwealth itself; the other, on account of his perpetual inconstancy in his popular policy, freed himself by a voluntary death from the severity of the judges. But each was a supreme orator.

And this we say with the memory of our fathers as witness; for we have speeches both of Carbo and of Gracchus, not yet sufficiently splendid in words, but acute and most full of good sense. Gracchus, by the diligence of his mother Cornelia, was taught from a boy and educated in Greek letters. For he always had choice teachers from Greece, and among them, when already a young man, Diophanes of Mytilene, the most eloquent man in Greece in those times. But the time for increasing and displaying his talent was short for him;

Carbo, to whom life was given in sufficiency, is known from many trials and causes. Those prudent men who had heard him — among whom our friend Lucius Gellius, who used to relate that he had been his tent-mate in his consulship — said that he was a melodious orator and fluent and keen enough, and at once vehement and very sweet and very witty; he added too that he was industrious and diligent, and was wont to put much effort into exercises and rehearsals.

He was held the best advocate in those times, and while he held the forum more trials began to take place. For both the standing courts were established when he was a young man, which before had been none — for Lucius Piso as tribune of the commons first carried the law on extortion in the consulship of Censorinus and Manilius; Piso himself too both pleaded causes and was the author or opposer of many laws, and he left both speeches, which have now faded, and annals written quite meagrely — and the trials before the people, at which Carbo was present, now needed an advocate more, once the ballot was given; which law Lucius Cassius carried in the consulship of Lepidus and Mancinus.

Your kinsman too, Decimus Brutus, son of Marcus — as I was wont to hear from his friend the poet Lucius Accius — used to speak not inelegantly and was learned both in Latin and Greek letters, as far as those times allowed. The same Accius ascribed these qualities also to Quintus Maximus, the grandson of Lucius Paullus; and indeed, before that Maximus, Scipio, under whose leadership as a private man Tiberius Gracchus was killed, he said was both vehement in all things and keen in speaking.

Then too that leading man Publius Lentulus is said to have had eloquence enough, at least so far as was needful for the commonwealth; and in those same times Lucius Furius Philus was thought to speak Latin very well and more learnedly than the rest; Publius Scaevola very prudently and acutely; a little more copiously, and not much less prudently, Manius Manilius. The oratory of Appius Claudius was fluent, but a little too heated. There were also of some account Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Cato, the son of Africanus's sister, middling orators; although there are writings of Flaccus, but as of a student of letters. And a rival of Flaccus was Publius Decius, not without speech indeed, but turbulent in his oratory as in his life.

Marcus Drusus, son of Gaius, who in his tribunate broke Gaius Gracchus, a tribune for the second time, was a man weighty both in oratory and in authority; and most nearly joined to him was his brother Gaius Drusus. Your clansman too, Brutus, Marcus Pennus, in his tribunate wittily harried Gaius Gracchus, going a little before him in age. For when Marcus Lepidus and Lucius Orestes were consuls, Gracchus was quaestor, Pennus tribune — the son of that Marcus who was consul with Quintus Aelius; but he, hoping for all the highest honours, died after holding the aedileship. For about Titus Flamininus, whom I myself saw, I have heard nothing except that he spoke Latin carefully.

To these are joined Gaius Curio, Marcus Scaurus, Publius Rutilius, Gaius Gracchus. About Scaurus and Rutilius one may speak briefly; neither of them had the praise of a supreme orator, and each was engaged in many causes. In certain men deserving praise, even if they were not of the greatest talent, their industry was nevertheless commendable; although in these indeed it was not talent altogether, but oratorical talent, that was lacking. For it is of no avail to see what should be said, unless you can say it fluently and agreeably; and not even that is enough, unless what is said is made more seasoned by voice, expression, and gesture.

And what need I say of learning? — without which, even if something is well said with nature helping, yet that, because it happens by chance, cannot always be ready. In the oratory of Scaurus, a wise and upright man, there was the highest weight and a certain natural authority, so that you would think, when he spoke for a defendant, that he was giving testimony rather than pleading a cause.

This kind of speaking seemed only moderately suited to advocacy, but to a senatorial opinion, of which he was the leading man, very much so; for it signified not prudence only, but — what most of all governed the matter — good faith. He had this from nature itself, which he could not easily have had from teaching; although of this very thing too, as you know, there are precepts. Of him there are both speeches and three books written to Lucius Fufidius on his own life, quite useful, which no one reads; but they read the life and education of Cyrus, that famous one indeed, but neither so suited to our affairs nor yet to be preferred to the praises of Scaurus.

Fufidius himself too was of some number among the advocates. Rutilius, however, was engaged in a certain grim and severe kind of speaking. Each was vehement and keen by nature; and so, when they had sought the consulship together, not only did the one who had suffered defeat accuse his elected competitor of bribery, but Scaurus too, when acquitted, summoned Rutilius into court. Rutilius was of much labour and much industry, which was the more welcome because the same man sustained the great office of giving answers on points of law.

His speeches are meagre; many of his observations on law are brilliant; a learned man and educated in Greek letters, a hearer of Panaetius, almost perfect among the Stoics — whose very acute and artful kind of oratory you nevertheless know to be thin and not well suited to popular assent. And so that opinion which is peculiar to this school — the philosophers' firm and unshaken opinion of themselves — was found in this man. For when, most innocent, he was summoned into court — by which trial we know that the commonwealth was deeply convulsed — although there were at that time the most eloquent men, Lucius Crassus and Marcus Antonius, of consular rank, he was unwilling to call in either of them. He pleaded for himself, and Gaius Cotta said a few words, because he was his sister's son — and he too, indeed, like an orator, although he was quite a young man — and Quintus Mucius spoke clearly indeed and politely, as was his wont, but by no means with that force and copiousness which the nature of that trial and the magnitude of the cause demanded.

We have, then, among the Stoic orators, Rutilius, among the antique, Scaurus; let us praise each, however, since through them not even these kinds in the state lacked this oratorical praise. For I would have it that, as on the stage, so also in the forum, not only those should be praised who use a quick and difficult action, but those too whom they call 'stationary,' whose virtue lies in that simple, unforced truth of pleading.

And since the Stoics have been mentioned, Quintus Aelius Tubero lived at that time, the grandson of Lucius Paullus; in no number of the orators, but severe in life and in keeping with that school which he cultivated, a little harsh too; who indeed in his tribunate gave judgement, against the testimony of his uncle Publius Africanus, that the augurs had no exemption from giving attention to trials; but harsh, uncultivated, rough in oratory as in life; and so he could not match the honours of his ancestors. He was, however, a steadfast and brave citizen, and among the foremost troublesome to Gracchus, which the speech of Gracchus against him indicates. There are also speeches of Tubero against Gracchus; he was middling in speaking, most learned in disputing." Then Brutus said,

"How I perceive that the same thing happens with our countrymen as with the Greeks — that nearly all the Stoics are most skilful in arguing and do it artfully and are almost architects of words, but the same, transferred from disputing to speaking, are found to be poor. I make one exception, Cato, in whom, as a most perfect Stoic, I would not miss the highest eloquence — which I see was scant in Fannius, not great even in Rutilius, and none at all in Tubero."

And I said, "Not without cause, Brutus, because all the care of those men is consumed in dialectic, and that wandering and diffuse and manifold kind of oratory is not employed. But your uncle, as you know, has from the Stoics what was to be sought from them; yet he learned to speak from the teachers of speaking, and trained himself in their manner. For if everything were to be sought from the philosophers, oratory would be better moulded by the instruction of the Peripatetics.

The more, then, do I approve your judgement, Brutus, who have followed the school of those philosophers — that is, of the Old Academy — in whose teaching and precepts the method of arguing is joined with sweetness and copiousness of speaking; although that very practice of the Peripatetics and Academics in the method of speaking is such that it can neither by itself perfect an orator, nor without it can the orator be perfect. For as the oratory of the Stoics is more compact and somewhat more contracted than the ears of the people require, so that of these is freer and broader than the custom of the courts and the forum allows. For who is more copious in speaking than Plato?

Jupiter, the philosophers say, if he spoke Greek, would speak so. Who is more sinewy than Aristotle, sweeter than Theophrastus? Demosthenes is said to have read Plato eagerly and even to have heard him — and this appears from the character and grandeur of his words; he says this himself of himself in a certain letter — but the oratory of the one, transferred to philosophy, seems more pugnacious, so to speak, and that of the others, transferred to the courts, more peaceful.

Now let us, if you please, trace the ages and degrees of the remaining orators." "Yes indeed," said Atticus, "and very eagerly, that I may answer for Brutus too." "Curio, then, of nearly the same age, was a really distinguished orator, whose talent can be judged from his speeches: for there are both others and the noble speech for Servius Fulvius on the charge of incest. When we were boys, this was thought the best of all, which now scarcely appears in this throng of new volumes."

"I know full well," said Brutus, "who has produced that throng of volumes." And I said, "I understand, Brutus, whom you mean; for certainly we both brought something good to the young men, a more magnificent kind of oratory than there had been and more ornate; and we did harm, perhaps, in that the old speeches, after ours — not by me, indeed, for I prefer them to my own — but by most people ceased to be read." "Count me," he said, "among the most; although I see I have now much to read, on your authority, which before I despised."

"And yet," I said, "this speech on incest, praised as it is, is boyish in many passages: on love, on tortures, on rumour the passages are quite empty, yet still tolerable in an age when the ears of our countrymen were not yet worn smooth and the state was not yet educated. He wrote some other things too and spoke many illustrious ones and was in the number of advocates, so that I wonder, since life had been granted him in sufficiency and splendour was not lacking to him, that he was not consul.

But behold, here is a man both of the most outstanding talent and of burning zeal, and learned from a boy — Gaius Gracchus. For do not suppose, Brutus, that anyone was fuller or richer for speaking." And he said, "So precisely do I judge, and of the earlier men I read him almost alone." "No," I said, "Brutus, read him, I advise you indeed plainly. For Roman affairs and Latin letters suffered loss by his untimely death.

Would that he had been willing to show his devotion to his country as much as to his brother! How easily, with such talent, had he lived longer, would he have attained either his father's or his grandfather's glory! In eloquence indeed I am inclined to think he would have had no equal. He is grand in words, wise in maxims, weighty in his whole kind. The finishing hand did not come to his works; many things admirably begun, not quite perfected. He is to be read, I say, by the young men, Brutus, if any orator is; for he can not only sharpen but also nourish the talent.

To this age succeeded Gaius Galba, the son of that most eloquent man Servius, the son-in-law of Publius Crassus, the eloquent and learned in law. Our fathers used to praise him, and favoured him too on account of his father's memory, but he fell in mid-course. For under the Mamilian bill, through the odium of the Jugurthine conspiracy, when he had pleaded for himself, he was overwhelmed. His peroration survives, which is called the epilogue; which was in such honour with us when we were boys that we even learned it by heart. He, being in a college of priests, was the first since the founding of Rome condemned in a public trial.

Publius Scipio, who died in his consulship, did not indeed speak much nor often, but in speaking Latin he was a match for anyone and surpassed all in wit and pleasantry. His colleague Lucius Bestia, starting from good beginnings in his tribunate — for he restored by his bill Publius Popilius, expelled by the violence of Gaius Gracchus — a man both keen and not without speech, had a sad end of his consulship. For by an odious law — the Mamilian inquiry — the Gracchan judges did away with Gaius Galba the priest and four consulars, Lucius Bestia, Gaius Cato, Spurius Albinus, and that most distinguished citizen Lucius Opimius, the slayer of Gracchus, though he had been acquitted by the people, since he had stood against the people's wish.

Unlike him in his tribunate and in all the rest of his life, a wicked citizen, Gaius Licinius Nerva was not without speech. Gaius Fimbria, of nearly the same times, but advanced further in age, was held, so to speak, a muddy advocate, harsh and abusive; in his whole kind a little too heated and excitable, yet by his diligence and the virtue of his mind and his life a good authority in the senate; likewise a tolerable advocate, not unskilled in civil law, and free both in his virtue and in the very kind of his oratory; whose speeches we read as boys, which now we can scarcely find.

And Gaius Sextius Calvinus was a man of keen talent and elegant speech, but of poor health; who, although, when the pains in his feet had relented, he was not wanting in causes, yet did not do this often. And so men used his counsel when they wished, his advocacy when it was permitted. In the same times Marcus Brutus — in whom there was a great disgrace, Brutus, to your family — who, although he bore so great a name and had had a most excellent father, most learned in law, made a regular trade of accusing, as Lycurgus did at Athens. He did not seek magistracies, but was a vehement and troublesome accuser, so that you could easily discern that a certain natural good of the stock had degenerated through the vice of a depraved will.

And at the same time there was an accuser from the commons, Lucius Caesulenus, whom I heard when he was already old, when he had claimed a fine from Lucius Sabellius under the Aquilian law. I would not have made mention of an almost lowest man, did I not judge that I had heard no one speak more suspiciously or more accusingly.

Learned in Greek too was Titus Albucius, or rather plainly a Greek. I speak as I think; but one may judge from his speeches. He was at Athens as a young man, and had come out a perfect Epicurean — a school least suited to speaking.

Now Quintus Catulus was learned, not in that ancient fashion, but in this of ours, than which nothing could be more perfect. Much learning, the highest courtesy not only of life and nature but of oratory too, a certain uncorrupted integrity of the Latin tongue; which can be perceived both from his speeches and most easily from that book which, written about his consulship and his own deeds in a soft and Xenophontic kind of style, he sent to the poet Aulus Furius, his friend; which book is no more known than those three books of Scaurus of which I spoke before.

Then Brutus said, "For my part I know neither that one nor those — but this is my own fault, for they never fell into my hands — but now I shall both take them from you and seek them out more carefully hereafter." "There was, then, in Catulus the Latin tongue; which praise of speaking, no small one, has been neglected by most orators. For as to the sound of his voice and the sweetness of pronouncing the letters, since you knew his son, do not wait to hear what I shall say. Although the son indeed was not in the number of the orators, yet he did not lack, in giving an opinion, both prudence and a certain elegant and learned kind of oratory.

Yet the father Catulus himself was not held the leading man in the number of advocates, but he was such that, when you heard certain men who were then preeminent, he seemed inferior, but when you heard him alone, without comparison, you were not only content but would not seek anything better.

Quintus Metellus Numidicus and his colleague Marcus Silanus used to speak about public affairs what was enough for such men and for consular dignity. Marcus Aurelius Scaurus did not speak often, but politely; in Latin indeed he spoke among the most elegant. The same praise of speaking well belonged to Aulus Albinus; for Albinus the flamen too was held in the number of able speakers. Quintus Caepio also, a keen and brave man, to whom the fortune of war was a charge and the people's hatred a calamity.

Then too Gaius and Lucius Memmius were middling orators, keen and bitter accusers; and so they summoned many to capital trial, but did not often plead for defendants. Spurius Thorius had power enough in the popular kind of speaking — he who relieved the public land by a faulty and useless rent-law. Marcus Marcellus, the father of Aeserninus, was not indeed among the advocates, but among the ready and not unpractised in speaking, as was his son

Publius Lentulus. Lucius Cotta too, of praetorian rank, in the number of middling orators, had not advanced very far in the praise of speaking, but of set purpose pursued and imitated antiquity, both in his words and even in the somewhat rustic sound of his speech.

And both in this Cotta himself and in many others I am aware that I both have entered, and shall enter, in the number of orators men not so very eloquent. For my purpose is to gather those who have discharged this office in the state, so as to hold the place of orators; and what their ascent was, and how difficult in all things is the perfection and finish of the best, may be judged from what I shall say.

For how many orators have now been mentioned, and how long are we engaged in their enumeration, when nevertheless slowly and scarcely — as a while ago to Demosthenes and Hyperides, so now to Antonius and Crassus — have we arrived! For so I judge, that these were the greatest orators, and that in them first the copiousness of speaking in Latin was made equal to the glory of the Greeks.

Everything came into Antonius's mind; and each thing was placed in its own place, where it could do most good and have most force — as by a general the cavalry, the infantry, the light-armed, so by him the parts of a speech were placed in their most advantageous positions. He had the highest memory, no suspicion of premeditation; he always seemed to approach speaking unprepared, but he was so prepared that, while he was speaking, the judges sometimes seemed to have been not sufficiently prepared to guard themselves.

The very words were indeed not of the most elegant diction — and so he lacked the praise of careful speaking, yet he did not speak at all foully — but those words which are the proper praise of an orator: for to speak Latin itself is, as I said a little before, to be reckoned among great merits, but not so much for its own sake as because it is neglected by most; for it is not so glorious to know Latin as it is disgraceful not to know it, nor does it seem to me so much the property of a good orator as of a Roman citizen; — but nevertheless Antonius, both in choosing words (and that itself not so much for charm as for weight) and in placing them and binding them together by their rounding-off, directed everything to method and, as it were, to art; but much more this same thing in the ornaments and shapings of the thoughts. And because Demosthenes excels all in this kind, he has therefore been judged by the learned the foremost of the orators. For the schemata, as the Greeks call them, most of all adorn the orator, and have their weight not so much in painting the words as in lighting up the thoughts.

But while these qualities were great in Antonius, his delivery too was singular; which, if it is to be divided into gesture and voice, his gesture was such as did not express the words but agreed with the thoughts: hands, shoulders, sides, stamping of the foot, posture, gait, and every movement in harmony with the words and thoughts; his voice lasting, but by nature somewhat hoarse. But this fault he alone turned to good.

For he had something tearful, suited both to producing belief and to stirring pity: so that there seemed to be truth in that saying which they relate of Demosthenes, who, when someone had asked what was first in speaking, answered 'delivery'; what second, the same; and the same a third time. Nothing penetrates more into men's minds and shapes, forms, and bends them, and makes the orators seem such as they themselves wish to seem.

Some said that Lucius Crassus was equal to him, others preferred him. This at least all judged thus, that there was no one who, with either of these as advocate, would feel the want of any other man's talent. For my part, although I assign so much to Antonius as I said above, yet I judge that nothing could have been made more perfect than Crassus. There was the highest dignity; there was joined with dignity an oratorical, not a buffoonish, charm of wit and urbanity; an accurate and unforced, careful elegance of speaking Latin; in arguing a marvellous power of exposition; when there was a debate about civil law, about the fair and the good, an abundance of arguments and comparisons.

For as Antonius had an incredible force in producing a conjecture or in allaying or arousing suspicion, so in interpreting, in defining, in unfolding equity, nothing was more copious than Crassus; and this was recognized, both often on other occasions and especially before the centumviri in the cause of Manius Curius.
