For there he said so much against the letter of the will in favour of the fair and the good that he overwhelmed that most acute man Quintus Scaevola, and most prepared in the law on which that cause turned, with an abundance of arguments and examples; and so that case was then pleaded by these advocates, of an age and now of consular rank, while each defended the civil law from the opposite side, in such a way that Crassus was thought the most learned in law of the eloquent, Scaevola the most eloquent of the learned in law. And Scaevola, although he was most acute in thinking out what in law or in equity was true or not, was yet wonderfully apt in words to the matter, with the greatest brevity.

Wherefore let us reckon him a marvellous orator in this kind of interpreting, explaining, expounding, so that I have seen nothing like it; but in amplifying, in adorning, in refuting, more an assessor to be feared than an orator to be admired. But let us return to Crassus." Then Brutus said,

"Although I seemed to myself to have known Scaevola well enough from those things which I often heard from Gaius Rutilius — whom I knew on account of his familiarity with our Scaevola — yet that great praise of his speaking was not known to me; and so I took pleasure that so accomplished a man and so excellent a talent existed in our commonwealth."

Here I said, "Do not, Brutus, suppose that anything was more excellent in our state than these two. For as I said a little before that the one was the most eloquent of the learned in law, the other the most learned in law of the eloquent, so in other respects they were so unlike each other that you could not nevertheless decide which you would rather resemble. Crassus was the most sparing of the elegant, Scaevola the most elegant of the sparing; Crassus, with the highest courtesy, had also severity enough, while Scaevola, with much severity, did not yet lack courtesy.

One may go on in this way with everything; but I fear these things may seem to be invented, so as to be said by me in a certain way; yet the matter stands thus. Since all virtue, as your Old Academy said, Brutus, is a mean, each of these wished to follow something middle; but it so fell out that the one had part of the other's praise, while each had his own praise entire."

Then Brutus said, "As, from your discourse, I seem to myself to have come to know Crassus and Scaevola well, so, thinking of you and of Servius Sulpicius, I judge that there is a certain likeness between you and them." "In what way, pray?" I said. "Because you too seem to me," he said, "to have wished to know just as much civil law as was enough for an orator, and Servius to have taken up just enough eloquence to be able easily to maintain the civil law; and your ages, like theirs, differ in nothing, or in next to nothing."

And I said, "About myself it is not necessary to say anything; but about Servius both you speak rightly, and I will say what I feel. For I could not easily name anyone who applied more zeal than he, both to speaking and to all the disciplines of good things. For we were engaged in the same exercises at the outset of our age, and afterwards he too set out together with me to Rhodes, that he might be better and more learned; and from the time he returned, he seems to me to have preferred to be first in the second art rather than second in the first. And I am inclined to think he might have been equal to the leading men; but perhaps he preferred — what he attained — to be by far the foremost of all, not only of those of his own age, but even of those who had ever been in the civil law.

Here Brutus said, "Do you say so? Do you set our Servius even before Quintus Scaevola?" "Thus indeed, Brutus, I judge," I said, "that there was a great practical use of civil law both in Scaevola and in many others, but the art in this one man alone; which the mere knowledge of law itself would never have produced, had he not besides learned that art which teaches one to divide a whole subject into parts, to unfold what is hidden by definition, to make plain what is obscure by interpretation, first to see ambiguities, then to distinguish them, and lastly to have a rule by which true and false may be judged, and what things follow from what premises and what do not.

For he brought this art, the greatest of all arts, as a kind of light to those things which were answered or pleaded confusedly by others." "You seem to me to mean dialectic," he said. "You understand rightly," I said; "but he joined to it also a knowledge of letters and an elegance of speech, which can most easily be perceived from his writings, of which there are none like them.

And since, for the sake of learning, he had studied under two most skilled men, Lucius Lucilius Balbus and Gaius Aquilius Gallus, he surpassed by his subtlety and diligence the ready and prepared quickness of Gallus, an acute and practised man, in pleading and in giving answers; and he overcame, in dispatching and finishing matters, the considered slowness of Balbus, a learned and erudite man, in both respects. So he has what each of them had, and supplied what each lacked.

And so, as Crassus seems to me to have acted more wisely than Scaevola — for the latter eagerly took up causes, in which he was surpassed by Crassus; the former did not wish to be consulted, lest in any matter he should be inferior to Scaevola — so Servius most wisely, since the two civil and forensic arts had the most of both praise and influence, brought it about that in the one he excelled all, and from the other took up just as much as was enough both to maintain the civil law and to obtain consular dignity.

Then Brutus said, "Just so, indeed, I thought before too — for I lately heard him eagerly and often at Samos, when I wished to learn from him our pontifical law, in so far as it was joined with the civil law — and now I confirm my judgement much more by your testimony and judgement; and at the same time I rejoice at this, that both your equality, and your equal ranks of honour, and the, as it were, neighbouring nearness of your arts and studies, are so far from that detraction and envy which is wont to tear most men, that it seems not only not to fester your mutual goodwill, but even to win it. For such as I perceive you to be toward him, such have I come to know him to be toward you in goodwill and judgement. And so I grieve that the Roman people lacks both his counsel and your voice for so long — which, while it is to be grieved over in itself, is much more so to one considering to whom these things have not been transferred, but have somehow come down." Here Atticus said, "I had said from the beginning that we should be silent about the commonwealth; so let us do so. For if we wish in this way to miss things one by one, we shall find an end not only of complaining but not even of mourning.

Let us proceed, then," I said, "to the rest, and pursue the order we have set." "Crassus, then, came prepared, was awaited, was listened to; from the very beginning at once — since with him everything was always careful — he seemed worthy of the expectation. There was not much throwing about of the body, no lowering of the voice, no walking about, no frequent stamping of the foot; his oratory was vehement and at times angry and full of just indignation, with much wit and that joined with weight; and — what is difficult — the same man was both very ornate and very brief; and now in altercation he found no equal.

He was engaged in nearly every kind of cause; he came early to the place of the leading orators. He accused Gaius Carbo, a most eloquent man, while quite a young man; he obtained the highest reputation of talent, not only praise but even admiration.

He afterwards defended the Vestal Licinia, when he was twenty-seven years old. In that very cause he was most eloquent, and left certain parts of his speech in writing. As a young man he wished to touch upon something of a popular cause in the colony of Narbo, and himself, as he did, to lead out that colony; there survives a speech of his on that law, more mature, so to speak, than that age bore. Then many causes; but his tribunate was so silent that, had he not in that magistracy dined at the house of the auctioneer Granius, and had Lucilius not twice told us this, we should not know that he had been tribune of the commons.

"Just so," said Brutus; "but neither do I seem to have heard anything of Scaevola's tribunate, and I believe he was a colleague of Crassus." "In all the other magistracies indeed," I said, "but Scaevola was tribune the year after, and with him sitting on the Rostra Crassus advocated the Servilian law; for he held the censorship without Scaevola — for that magistracy none of the Scaevolae ever sought. But this speech of Crassus, when it was published — which I know for certain you have often read — he was then thirty-four years old, and exceeded me in age by just as many years. For he advocated that law in the consulship of those in which we were born, since he himself was born in the consulship of Quintus Caepio and Gaius Laelius, just three years younger than Antonius. Which I have set down for this reason — that it might be noted in what age the first maturity of speaking Latin appeared, and that it might be understood that it had now been brought almost to its summit, so that scarcely anyone could add anything to it, except one who should be better furnished from philosophy, from civil law, from history."

"Is there, or is there already," said Brutus, "that man whom you await?" "I do not know," I said. "But there is also a speech of Lucius Crassus in his consulship for Quintus Caepio, a joined defence, not brief as a eulogy, but, as a speech, brief; and his last, as censor, which he used in his forty-eighth year. In all these there is a certain colour of truth without any paint; nay more, that grouping and rounding-off of words — if it pleases to call it thus a 'period' — was with him contracted and brief, and he distributed his oratory rather gladly into certain members, which the Greeks call cola.

At this point Brutus said, "Since you praise those orators so highly, I could wish that Antonius had pleased to write something more besides that quite meagre little book on the method of speaking, and Crassus more: for they would have left to all a memorial of themselves, and to us besides a discipline of speaking. For we have come to know the elegance of Scaevola's speaking sufficiently from those speeches which he left."

And I said, "For my part, from boyhood that speech on the law of Caepio was, as it were, my mistress; in which both the authority of the senate is adorned, on whose behalf, as an order, those things are said, and odium is roused against the faction of the judges and of the accusers, against whose power one then had to speak in a popular manner. In that speech many things were said weightily, many gently, many harshly, many wittily; more even were said than were written, as can be understood from certain heads set down but not developed. That censorial speech itself against his colleague Gnaeus Domitius is not a speech, but, as it were, heads of matters and a somewhat fuller note for the speech. For there was never an altercation held with greater outcry.
And indeed in this man too the popular style of speaking was excellent; the kind of speaking of Antonius was much more suited to the courts than to public assemblies.

At this point I do not leave out Domitius himself. For although he was not in the number of the orators, yet I judge that there was enough of oratory and talent in him to maintain both the part of a magistrate and consular dignity; the same I would say of Gaius Caelius, that there was in him the highest industry and the highest virtues, and just so much eloquence as was enough for his friends in private affairs, and for his own dignity in public affairs. At the same time Marcus Herennius was counted among the middling orators who spoke Latin carefully; who nevertheless surpassed in the canvass for the consulship Lucius Philippus, a man of the highest nobility, by kinship, fellowship, college, and the highest eloquence too. At the same time Gaius Claudius, although he was great on account of his highest nobility and singular power, yet brought also a certain middling eloquence. Of nearly the same time was the Roman knight

Gaius Titius, who in my judgement seems to have arrived where a Latin orator could nearly arrive without Greek letters and without much practice. His speeches have so much pointedness, so many examples, so much urbanity, that they seem almost written in the Attic style. The same pointed wit he transferred to tragedies acutely enough, but with too little of the tragic. Him the poet Lucius Afranius was eager to imitate, a very pointed man, eloquent indeed even in his plays, as you know.

There was also Quintus Rubrius Varro, who was judged by the senate a public enemy along with Gaius Marius, a keen and vehement accuser, in that kind quite commendable. Learned too in Greek letters and made for speaking was our kinsman Marcus Gratidius, a close friend of Marcus Antonius, while whose prefect he was killed in Cilicia; he it was who accused Gaius Fimbria — the father of Marcus Marius Gratidianus.

And even among the allies and Latins there were held to be orators: Quintus Vettius Vettianus of the Marsi, whom I myself knew, a prudent man and brief in speaking; the Quintus and Decimus Valerius of Sora, my neighbours and friends, not so admirable in speaking as learned both in Greek and Latin letters; Gaius Rusticelius of Bononia, he indeed both practised and naturally fluent; but the most eloquent of all outside this city was Titus Betucius Barrus of Asculum, of whom there are some speeches delivered at Asculum, and one at Rome against Caepio, quite noble; to which speech Aelius answered through the mouth of Caepio — Aelius who regularly wrote speeches for many, but was never an orator himself.

Among our ancestors, however, I find that Lucius Papirius of Fregellae was held the most eloquent from Latium, of nearly the age of Tiberius Gracchus, son of Publius; of him there is also a speech delivered in the senate for the people of Fregellae and the Latin colonists." Then Brutus said, "What, then, do you assign to those foreign orators, as it were?" "What do you think," I said, "except the same as to the city ones? — except for one thing, that their oratory is not, as it were, coloured by a certain urbanity." And Brutus said,

"What, pray, is that colour of urbanity?" "I do not know," I said; "I only know that there is a certain something. This you, Brutus, will already understand, when you come into Gaul; you will hear there even certain words not current at Rome, but these can be changed and unlearned; that other thing is greater, which in the voices of our orators rings and resounds more urbanely. Nor does this appear in orators only, but in others too.

I remember that Titus Tinca of Placentia, a most witty man, used to contend in raillery with our friend the auctioneer Quintus Granius." "Is it he," said Brutus, "about whom Lucilius says much?" "That very man; but Granius, though Tinca said no fewer laughable things, overwhelmed him with a certain native flavour; so that I no longer wonder at that which is said to have happened to Theophrastus, who, when he was inquiring of a certain old woman at what price she was selling something, and she had answered and added, 'Stranger, it cannot be less,' took it ill that he did not escape the appearance of a stranger, though he had passed his life at Athens and spoke best of all. So, as I think, in our people there is a certain sound of the city folk, as there of the Athenians. But let us return home — that is, let us go back to our own.

To the two highest, then, Crassus and Antonius, Lucius Philippus came nearest, but nearest by a long interval, nevertheless. And so, although no one came between to set himself before him, yet I would call him neither second nor third. For in a chariot-race I would not count him second or third who has scarcely come out of the starting-stalls when the first has already received the palm; nor among orators one who is so far from the first that he scarcely seems to be on the same course. But yet there were in Philippus those qualities which, were one to regard them without comparison with those men, he would call great enough: the highest freedom in speech, much wit; frequent enough in discovering his thoughts, fluent in unfolding them; he was also among the foremost, for those times, instructed in Greek learning, and in altercation witty with a certain sting and abuse.

Almost joined to the age of these was Lucius Gellius, an orator not so much in demand, although you would not know what was lacking to him; for he was neither unlearned nor slow at devising, nor unmindful of Roman affairs, and fluent enough in words; but his age had fallen among great orators. Yet he gave much and useful service to his friends, and lived so long that he was bound up with the orators of many ages.

Much engaged in causes too, at nearly the same times, was Decimus Brutus, he who was consul with Mamercus, a man learned both in Greek and Latin letters. Lucius Scipio too spoke not unskilfully, and Gnaeus Pompeius, son of Sextus, held some rank. For Sextus his brother had devoted a most outstanding talent to the highest knowledge of civil law and to a perfect knowledge of geometry and of Stoic matters. Likewise in law, and before these, Marcus Brutus, and a little after him Gaius Billienus, a man great by himself, had come out, by nearly a similar method, supreme; who would have been made consul, had he not fallen upon the Marian consulships and upon those straits of canvassing.

But the eloquence of Gnaeus Octavius, which had been unknown before his consulship, was in his consulship vehemently approved in many assemblies. But from those who were only in the number of speakers, not of orators, let us now return to the orators." "I agree," said Atticus; "for you seemed to wish to seek out the eloquent, not the diligent."

"In festivity, then, and in wit," I said, "Gaius Julius, son of Lucius, surpassed all his elders and all his equals, and was an orator not at all vehement indeed, but no one was ever more seasoned with urbanity, with charm, with sweetness. There are some speeches of his, from which, as from his tragedies of the same kind, his gentleness, not without sinew, can be perceived.

His equal Publius Cethegus, for whom there was speech enough about public affairs — for he held it and had come to know it thoroughly; and so in the senate he obtained the authority of consulars — but in public causes he seemed nothing, in private ones an old hand enough. In private causes there was Quintus Lucretius Vispillo, both acute and skilled in law; for Ofella was more suited to assemblies than to courts. Prudent too was Titus Annius Velina, and in causes of that kind a quite tolerable orator. In the same kind of causes much engaged was Titus Iuventius, too slow indeed in speaking and almost frigid, but both shrewd and cunning in catching his adversary, and besides not unlearned, and with a great understanding of civil law.

His hearer Publius Orbius, of nearly my own age, was not very practised in speaking, but in civil law was not inferior to his teacher. For Titus Aufidius, who lived to extreme old age, wished to be like these men, and was both a good and an innocent man, but spoke too little; nor indeed more did his brother Marcus Vergilius, who as tribune of the commons cited the commander Lucius Sulla to appear. His colleague Publius Magius was nevertheless a little more copious in speaking.

But of all the orators, or rather ranters, who were plainly unlearned and inurbane or even rustic, of those at least whom I have known, I judge the most fluent and the most acute in speaking, of our order, Quintus Sertorius, of the equestrian, Gaius Gargonius. There was also one easy and ready for speaking, of much splendour of life and quite commendable talent, Titus Junius, son of Lucius, of tribunician rank, on whose accusation Publius Sextius, praetor-elect, was condemned for bribery; he would have advanced further in honours, had he not always been of a feeble and even sickly health.

And I perfectly well understand that I am engaged in mentioning men who were neither held to be orators nor were so, and that some are passed over by me from among the old men who deserved mention or praise. But this is through ignorance; for what is there of an earlier age that can be written about those of whom no monuments speak, neither of others nor of themselves? But of those whom we ourselves have seen, we shall pass over almost no one [of those whom we have at some time seen speaking].

For I wish it to be known that, in so great and so old a commonwealth, with the greatest rewards of eloquence set forth, all desired to speak, not very many ventured, few were able. Yet I shall speak of each one in such a way that it can be understood whom I judge to have been a bawler, whom an orator. At nearly the same times, a little younger than Julius, but almost his equals, were Gaius Cotta, Publius Sulpicius, Quintus Varius, Gnaeus Pomponius, Gaius Curio, Lucius Fufius, Marcus Drusus, Publius Antistius; nor was there ever a richer crop of orators in any age.

Of these Cotta and Sulpicius, in my judgement and easily in that of all, bore away the first place." Here Atticus said, "How do you mean that — both in your judgement and in that of all? Does the judgement of the crowd, in approving or disapproving an orator, always agree with the judgement of those who understand? Or are some approved by the multitude, others by those who understand?" "You inquire rightly, Atticus," I said; "but you will perhaps hear from me what not all may approve.

"Do you trouble yourself about that," he said, "if you are about to win the approval only of Brutus here?" "Plainly, Atticus," I said, "I would much rather that this disputation about approving or disapproving an orator should please you and Brutus, but I would have my own eloquence approved by the people. For he who so speaks as to be approved by the multitude must necessarily be approved by the learned too. For what in speaking is right or faulty I shall judge, if only I am such as can or know how to judge it; but what kind of orator he is can be understood from what he accomplishes by speaking.

For there are three things, as I at least feel, which are to be accomplished by speaking: that the one before whom one speaks should be instructed, that he should be delighted, that he should be vehemently moved. By what virtues of an orator each of these is accomplished, or by what faults the orator either does not attain these or even slips and falls in them, some artist will judge. But whether or not it is accomplished by the orator that those who hear are so affected as the orator wishes, is wont to be judged by the assent of the crowd and the approbation of the people. And so there was never a disagreement between the learned and the people about a good orator or a bad one.

Do you think that, while those flourished whom I mentioned before, the gradations of orators were not the same in the judgement of the crowd and of the learned? If you had asked anyone from the people, 'Who is the most eloquent in this state?' he would either hesitate between Antonius and Crassus, or one would name this one, another that. Would no one set before these Philippus, so sweet an orator, so weighty, so witty — whom we ourselves, who wish to weigh these things by some art, have said to have been nearest to them? Surely no one; for this very thing is the mark of the supreme orator, to seem to the people the supreme orator.

Wherefore, as the flute-player Antigenidas said to a pupil who was failing badly with the people, 'Play for me and for the Muses,' so I would say to Brutus here, speaking, as he is wont, before the multitude, 'Play for me and for the people, my Brutus,' that those who hear may know what is accomplished, and I too may understand why it is accomplished. He who hears an orator believes what is said, thinks it true, assents, approves; the speech produces belief: you, the artist, what more do you seek?

The hearing multitude is delighted and led by the speech and, as it were, suffused with a certain pleasure: what have you to dispute? It rejoices, grieves, laughs, weeps, favours, hates, despises, envies, is led to pity, to shame, to regret; it is angered, mollified, hopes, fears; these things happen just as the minds of those present are handled by words and thoughts and delivery; what is there that should await the opinion of some learned man? For what the multitude approves, this same thing the learned must approve. In short, this is the proof of the people's judgement, in which there was never a disagreement of the people with the learned and the understanding.

When there were many orators of varied kinds of speaking, which of these was ever judged to excel by the judgement of the crowd, who was not likewise approved by the learned? And when would it have been doubtful among our fathers, to whom the choice was given of an advocate, that he should choose either Antonius or Crassus? Many others were at hand; yet which of these one might have rather doubted about, but that of the two no one doubted. And when, in our youth, there were Cotta and Hortensius, did anyone, who at least had the power of choosing, prefer anyone to these?

Then Brutus said, "Why do you seek others? About yourself, did we not see what defendants would wish, what Hortensius himself judged? — who, when he shared causes with you — for I was often present — always left to you the place of peroration, where oratory is most powerful." "He did that indeed," I said, "and, led, I believe, by goodwill toward me, ascribed everything to me. But what the people's opinion of me may be I do not know; about the rest I affirm this, that those who were held in the opinion of the crowd the most eloquent were the same most approved in the judgement of the understanding too.

For Demosthenes could not say the same as they relate the famous poet Antimachus to have said: who, when, his hearers having been called together, he read to them that great volume of his which you know, and when all except Plato had left him reading, said, 'I shall read none the less: for to me Plato alone is worth a hundred thousand.' And rightly; for a recondite poem ought to move the approbation of a few, a popular speech the assent of the crowd. But if Demosthenes had this same Plato as his single hearer, when he had been left by the rest, he could not have uttered a word.

What could you do, Brutus, if an assembly should leave you, as it once left Curio?" "For my part," said he, "to declare myself to you, even in those causes in which all our business is with the judges, not with the people, yet if I should be left by the bystanders, I could not speak." "So the matter stands," I said. "As, if blown flutes do not return their sound, the flute-player thinks they should be thrown away, so to the orator the people's ears are, as it were, flutes; if these do not receive the breath blown into them — or if the hearer altogether, like a horse, does not respond — an end must be made of driving.

There is this difference, however, that the crowd sometimes approves an orator who ought not to be approved, but approves him without comparison; when it is delighted by a middling or even a bad one, it is content with him; it does not perceive that there is better; it approves that which is, of whatever kind it is. For even a middling orator holds the ears, provided there is something in him; nor does anything have more force with men's minds than the order and ornament of oratory.

Wherefore who from the people, when he heard Quintus Scaevola speaking for Marcus Coponius in that cause of which I spoke before, would either expect anything more polished or more elegant or altogether better, or think that it could be made?

When he wished to prove this — that Manius Curius, when he had been so instituted heir, 'if the ward should have died before he came into his own guardianship,' could not be heir, the ward not having been born — what did he not say about the law of wills? about the old formulae? how it ought to have been written, if an heir were instituted even in case the son were not born?
how captious it was for the people, that what was written should be neglected, and intentions sought by conjecture, and the writings of simple men perverted by the interpretation of the eloquent?

how much he said about the authority of his father, who had always maintained that this was the law? how much altogether about preserving the civil law? And when he said all these things both skilfully and knowingly, and likewise briefly and closely and ornately enough and very elegantly, who would there be among the people who would either expect or think that anything could be made better? But indeed, as on the other side Crassus began with a young dandy who, walking on the shore and having found an oar-pin, conceived a desire to build a ship on that account, that Scaevola likewise had from one oar-pin made a centumviral trial of an inheritance: by this beginning, with many thoughts of the same kind following, he delighted and led the minds of all who were present from severity to mirth — which is one of the three things which I said must be accomplished by an orator. Then that the man who had made the will had wished this, had meant this, that in whatever way there should be no son to come into his own guardianship, whether unborn or dead before, Curius should be heir; that most men so write, and that this is valid and always has been valid. Saying these things and many of the kind, he produced belief; which is the second of the three duties of an orator.

Then he maintained the fair and good intentions and wishes of wills: how great the captiousness in words would be, both in other matters and especially in wills, if intentions were neglected; how great a power Scaevola would assume to himself, if no one should dare to make a will hereafter except according to his opinion. Unfolding these things both weightily and copiously with examples, and with variety, and even laughably and wittily, he stirred such admiration and assent that it seemed no one had spoken on the other side; — this was the third duty of the orator by division, the greatest in kind. Here that judge from the people, who separately had admired the one, would, when he had heard the other, despise his own judgement; but the understanding and learned hearer, listening to Scaevola, would feel that there was a certain richer and more ornate kind of speaking. But when the cause had been pleaded by each, if it were asked which was the better orator, never indeed would the judgement of the wise man differ from the judgement of the crowd.

In what, then, does the understanding man surpass the unskilled? In a great and difficult thing; if indeed it is great to know by what means is accomplished or lost in speaking that, whatever it is, which either ought to be accomplished by speaking or ought not to be lost. The learned hearer surpasses the unlearned in this too, that often, when two or more orators are approved by the people's judgement, he understands which kind of speaking is best. For that which is not approved by the people cannot be approved even by the understanding hearer. For as from the sound of the strings in the lyre it is wont to be understood how skilfully they have been struck, so from the movement of minds it is discerned what the orator accomplishes in handling them.

And so the understanding judge of speaking, not sitting by and listening attentively, but at a single glance and in passing, often judges of the orator. He sees the judge yawning, talking with another, sometimes even forming a knot of bystanders, sending to ask the hour, asking the president to dismiss the court: he understands that there is no orator present in that cause who can apply his oratory to the minds of the judges as the hand to the lyre. The same man, if in passing he has seen the judges intent and looking up, so that they seem either to be instructed about the matter and to approve it even by their expression, or, as a bird by some song, to be held, as it were, suspended by the oratory, or — what is most needed — to be more vehemently disturbed by pity, hatred, or some movement of the mind: if, in passing, as I said, he has seen these things, though he has heard nothing, he will surely understand that an orator is at work in that trial and that an oratorical work is being done or is already finished."

When I had set forth these things, each assented; and I, as if beginning anew, said, "Since, then, all this discourse flowed from Cotta and Sulpicius, when I said that these were most approved by the judgement of those men and of that age, I shall return to them themselves; then I shall pursue the rest in order, as I have begun. Since, then, there are two kinds of good orators — for these are what we are seeking — one of those who speak thinly and closely, the other of those who speak loftily and amply; although that is better which is more splendid and magnificent, yet in good men all things that are of the highest are rightly praised.

But that close orator must beware of poverty and meagreness, the ample one of an inflated and corrupt kind of oratory. Cotta, then, discovered acutely, spoke purely and fluently; and as, very knowingly, on account of the weakness of his sides, he had relaxed all straining, so to the feebleness of his strength he accommodated his kind of speaking. There was nothing in his oratory but what was genuine, nothing but what was dry and sound; and this was the greatest thing, that, although he could scarcely bend the minds of the judges by force of oratory and did not speak at all in that kind, yet by his handling he impelled them to do the same, moved by him, as those roused by Sulpicius did.

For Sulpicius was, of all whom at least I have heard, perhaps the most grand and, so to speak, tragic orator. His voice was both great and sweet and splendid; his gesture and the movement of his body so graceful that he nevertheless seemed trained for the forum, not for the stage; his oratory impetuous and fluent, yet not redundant nor overflowing. He wished to imitate Crassus; Cotta preferred Antonius; but from the latter the force of Antonius was absent, from the former the charm of Crassus."

"O great art!" said Brutus; "if indeed in those men, when they were supreme orators, each lacked one of the two greatest things which the other had." "And in these orators this is to be noted, that they can be supreme who are unlike each other. For nothing was so unlike as Cotta to Sulpicius, and each greatly excelled his equals. Wherefore it is the part of an understanding teacher to see whither each man's nature carries him, and, using that as a guide, so to train him — as it is recorded that Isocrates said, of the very keen talent of Theopompus and the very gentle one of Ephorus, that he applied spurs to the one, reins to the other.

The speeches of Sulpicius which are in circulation, Publius Cannutius, my contemporary, a man in my judgement most eloquent outside our order, is thought to have written after his death. Of Sulpicius himself there is no speech, and I often heard from him that he was neither accustomed nor able to write. The speech of Cotta for himself under the Varian law, as it is entitled, Lucius Aelius wrote at Cotta's request. He was altogether an excellent man and a Roman knight most honourable among the first, and likewise most learned both in Greek and Latin letters, and lettered and skilled in our antiquity, both in things discovered and in things done and in the old writers. This knowledge our Varro, a man of outstanding talent and of every learning, received from him and increased by himself, and set forth in fuller and more illustrious writings.

But the same Aelius wished to be a Stoic, and as an orator he never either studied or was one. Yet he wrote speeches for others to deliver; as for Quintus Metellus, for Quintus Caepio, for Quintus Pompeius Rufus — although the latter himself also wrote those which he used for himself, but not without Aelius.

For at these writings I myself was present, when I was a young man with Aelius and used to hear him very eagerly. But I wonder that Cotta, himself a supreme orator and least inept, was willing for the slight little speeches of Aelius to be thought his own.

To these two of the same age no third was counted, but Pomponius pleased me most, or rather, displeased me least. There was altogether a place in the greatest causes for no one besides those of whom I spoke above, because Antonius, who was most sought after, was easy in accepting causes; Crassus more fastidious, but he too accepted them. He who had neither of these took refuge generally with Philippus or with Caesar; Cotta and Sulpicius were sought after. So by these six advocates the illustrious causes were pleaded; and there were not so many trials as in our age, nor what now happens, that single causes were defended by several — than which nothing is more faulty.

We answer those whom we have not heard: in which, first, often one thing was said and another reported to us; then it is of great importance that I should see for myself how my adversary asserts about each matter, and especially how each matter is received. But nothing is more faulty than that, when there ought to be one body of the defence, the cause should arise anew, when it has been concluded by another.

For of all causes there is one natural beginning, one peroration; the remaining parts, as members each placed in its own place, hold their own force and dignity. And since it is difficult in a long speech not sometimes to say something so that one is inconsistent with oneself, how much more difficult is it to beware of saying anything that is not consistent with the speech of him who spoke before you? But because both the labour is much greater to plead a whole cause than a part, and because more thanks are won if you speak at one time for several, therefore we have gladly adopted this custom.

There were, however, some to whom Curio seemed the third of that age, because he perhaps used more splendid words and because he spoke Latin not at all badly, owing, I believe, to some domestic usage. For of letters he knew almost nothing; but it is of great importance whom one hears daily at home, with whom one converses from a boy, how fathers, tutors, and even mothers speak. We read the letters of Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi: it appears that the sons were brought up not so much in the lap as in the speech of their mother. The speech of Laelia, daughter of Gaius, was often heard by us: therefore we saw her tinged with the elegance of her father, and his two daughters the Muciae, whose speech was known to me, and his granddaughters the Liciniae, both of whom we ourselves heard, and the wife of Scipio you too, Brutus, I believe, heard speaking at some time." "Yes indeed, and gladly," said Brutus; "and the more gladly because she was the daughter of Lucius Crassus."

"What of that Crassus," I said, "the son of that Licinia, who was adopted by the will of Crassus?" "He is said indeed to have been of the highest talent," he said; "and indeed this Scipio, my colleague, seems to me really both to speak and to plead well." "You judge rightly, Brutus," I said. "For his stock is begotten from the very root of wisdom. For we have already spoken of his two grandfathers, Scipio and Crassus, and of his three great-grandfathers, Quintus Metellus, of those famous four sons, Publius Scipio, who from the domination of Tiberius Gracchus, as a private man, reclaimed the commonwealth into liberty, and Quintus Scaevola the augur, who was held most skilled in law and likewise very affable. And how illustrious is the name of his two great-great-grandfathers,

Publius Scipio, who was twice consul, who was called Corculum, and the other the wisest of all, Gaius Laelius." "O noble stock," he said, "and, as into one tree several kinds are grafted, so into that house the engrafted wisdom of many!" "Similarly, then, I surmise — to compare small things with great — that the house of Curio, although he was left an orphan, was, by his father's example, accustomed to pure speech; and I judge this the more because I have known no one of those at least who were of any account so unlearned, so rude in every kind of honourable arts.

He had known no poet, had read no orator, had collected no memory of antiquity; he had learned neither public nor private and civil law. Although this indeed was the case in others too, and great orators indeed, whom we saw too little furnished with these arts, such as Sulpicius, such as Antonius. But they nevertheless had that one work of speaking elaborated; and since it consists of five very well-known parts, no one could be utterly nothing in any part of them: for in whichever single one he plainly limped, he could not be an orator; but yet one excelled more in one, another in another.

Antonius found what needed to be said and how it should be prepared and in what place placed, and embraced these in his memory, but excelled in delivery; and he had some of these on a par with Crassus, some even superior; but the oratory of Crassus shone more. Nor indeed can we say that to Sulpicius or to Cotta or to any good orator any one of those five parts was plainly and utterly lacking.

And so in Curio this can most truly be judged, that an orator is commended by no one thing more than by the splendour and copiousness of his words. For he was both slow in thinking and disordered in arranging. The remaining two are delivery and memory: in each he stirred the guffaws of those who mocked. His movement was such as both Gaius Julius marked for ever — when, as he swayed his whole body to either side, he asked who was speaking from a boat — and Gnaeus Sicinius, an impure but very ridiculous man; nor was there anything else in him resembling an orator.

When, as tribune of the commons, he had brought forward the consuls Curio and Octavius, and Curio had said much while his colleague Gnaeus Octavius sat by, who was bound with bandages and smeared with many medicaments on account of the pain in his limbs, Sicinius said: 'Never, Octavius, will you repay thanks to your colleague: who, had he not tossed himself about in his manner, the flies would have eaten you up there today.' His memory was so utterly none that sometimes, when he had proposed three things, he would either add a fourth or look for the third; who, in a private trial, even a very great one, when I had concluded for Titinia, the wife of Cotta, and he was speaking against me for Servius Naevius, suddenly forgot the whole cause, and said that this had been done by the poisons and enchantments of Titinia. Great signs these of a forgetful mind; but nothing is more shameful than that even in his writings he forgot what he had set down a little before — as in that book where he represents himself coming out of the senate and conversing with our Pansa and with the younger Curio, and all that conversation is drawn from the son's inquiry about what had been done in the senate. In which, when Curio inveighed at length against Caesar, and there was a discussion between them, as is the custom of dialogues, since the conversation was begun after the dismissal of the senate which Caesar as consul had held, he censured those things which the same Caesar administered in Gaul a year later and afterwards in the remaining years.

Then Brutus, wondering, said, "Was there so great a forgetfulness, especially in writing, that not even in reading did he ever perceive how great a disgrace he had committed?" "And what," I said, "Brutus, more foolish than, if he wished to censure those things which he censured, not to set the conversation at a time when the times of those things had already passed? But he so wholly errs that in the same conversation he says that he does not enter the senate while Caesar is consul, and says this as he is going out of the senate while that very man is consul. Now, one who in this part of the mind, which is the guardian of the other parts of the talent, was so feeble that not even in writing did he remember what he had set down a little before — for him it is least to be wondered at that, speaking off-hand, his mind was wont to slip away.

And so, although he did not lack official position and burned with zeal for speaking, very few causes were brought to him. As an orator, however, he was counted nearest the best of the living of his age, on account of the goodness of his words, as I said before, and a certain ready and flowing quickness. And so I judge that his speeches should nevertheless be looked at. They are indeed rather languid, but yet they can increase and, as it were, nourish that good which we grant was in him in middling measure: which has such force that alone, without the others, it produced in Curio the appearance of some sort of orator. But let us return to our plan.

In the same number, then, of the same age was Gaius Carbo, the son of that most eloquent man. Not a sufficiently acute orator, but yet counted an orator. There was weight in his words, and he spoke easily, and his oratory had a certain natural authority. More acute was Quintus Varius in finding matter, and no less ready in words; a strong pleader and vehement, and neither poor nor mean in words, and one whom you would plainly dare to call an orator was Gnaeus Pomponius, fighting with his sides, rousing minds, keen, bitter, accusing.

Much inferior to these was Lucius Fufius, who nevertheless from the accusation of Manius Aquilius had reaped the fruit of his diligence. For your great-uncle Marcus Drusus, a weighty orator only so far as when he spoke about public affairs; and Lucius Lucullus, even acute; and your father, Brutus, quite skilled too both in public and private law; Marcus Lucullus; Marcus Octavius, son of Gnaeus, who was so strong in authority and in speaking that he repealed the Sempronian corn-law by the votes of a crowded people; Gnaeus Octavius, son of Marcus; Marcus Cato the father; and Quintus Catulus the son too — let us lead out of the battle-line, that is, from the courts, and place in the garrisons of the commonwealth, which they can easily satisfy.

To the same I would refer Quintus Caepio, had he not, too devoted to the equestrian order, dissented from the senate. Gnaeus Carbo, Marcus Marius, and several of the same kind, least worthy of the ears of an elegant assembly, I have known most fitted to turbulent gatherings. In which kind — to disturb here the order of ages — was lately Lucius Quinctius; more suited even to the ears of the unskilled was Palicanus.

And since mention has been made of this kind, of all the seditious men after the Gracchi Lucius Appuleius Saturninus seemed the most eloquent; yet he caught men more by his appearance and movement and his very dress than by copiousness of speaking or by middling prudence. By far the most wicked since the birth of men was Gaius Servilius Glaucia, but very acute and shrewd and among the foremost ridiculous. He, from the lowest depths both of fortune and of life, in his praetorship would have been made consul, had it been judged lawful for his candidacy to be taken into account. For he both held the commons and had bound the equestrian order to himself by the benefit of a law. He as praetor, on the same day on which Saturninus the tribune of the commons, in the consulship of Marius and Flaccus, was publicly killed; a man most like the Athenian Hyperbolus, whose wickedness the old comedies of the Athenians marked.

These Sextus Titius followed, a talkative man indeed and acute enough, but so loose and soft in gesture that a certain dance was born, to which dance the name 'Titius' was given. So one must beware of doing anything in pleading or speaking, the imitation of which may be laughed at. But we have gone back to a somewhat earlier age; now let us return to that of which we have spoken a good deal.

Joined, then, to the age of Sulpicius was Publius Antistius, a quite commendable ranter, who, after he had been silent for many years and had been wont not only to be despised but even mocked, in his tribunate was first approved, pleading the true cause against that extraordinary candidacy of Gaius Julius for the consulship; and the more because, when his colleague that very Sulpicius pleaded the same cause, this man said more and more acute things. And so after his tribunate at first many causes were brought to him, then all the greatest, whatever they were.

He saw the matter acutely, arranged it diligently, was strong in memory; he used words not indeed ornate but yet not mean; his oratory was ready and ran very easily; and he had a certain bearing, as it were, not inurbane; his delivery limped a little both with a fault of voice and with ineptitudes. He flourished in those times when, between the departure and return of Lucius Sulla, the commonwealth was without law and without any dignity; he was the more approved for this too, that there was a certain solitude of orators in the forum. Sulpicius had fallen, Cotta was away and Curio, of the remaining advocates of that age none was living except Carbo and Pomponius, both of whom he easily surpassed.

Of a lower age the nearest was Lucius Sisenna, a learned man and devoted to the best studies, speaking good Latin, acquainted with public affairs, not without wit, but neither of much labour nor sufficiently versed in causes; and set between the two ages of Hortensius and Sulpicius, he could neither attain the greater nor had necessarily to yield to the lesser. His whole faculty can be perceived from his history, which, while it easily surpasses all earlier ones, yet shows how far it is from the highest and how this kind of writing is not yet sufficiently illuminated in Latin letters. For the talent of Quintus Hortensius, while a very young man, was at once, like a statue of Phidias, looked upon and approved. He first spoke in the forum in the consulship of Lucius Crassus and Quintus Scaevola, and before these very consuls indeed, and he came away approved by the judgement both of those who were present and of the consuls themselves, who surpassed all in understanding. He was nineteen years old at that time, but died in the consulship of Lucius Paullus and Gaius Marcellus: from which we see that he was in the number of advocates for forty-four years. About this orator we shall say more a little later; but in this place we wished to include his age within the unequal age of the orators. Although this indeed necessarily befell all to whom a somewhat longer life fell, that they were compared both with men much older than themselves and with some considerably younger. As Accius says that under the same aediles both he and Pacuvius produced a play, when the latter was eighty and he himself thirty years old: so

Hortensius is joined not only with his own equals but with my age and with yours, Brutus, and with one considerably earlier, if indeed he was wont to speak while Crassus was living, and was now even more in vigour when Antonius and Philippus, now an old man, pleaded for the property of Gnaeus Pompeius in that cause, where, though he was a young man, he was the leading speaker; and he had easily come into the number of those whom I placed in the age of Sulpicius, and among his own equals — Marcus Piso, Marcus Crassus, Gnaeus Lentulus, Publius Lentulus Sura — he far excelled, and, having got me as a young man eight years younger than he was himself, he exercised me for many years in the pursuit of the same praise, and together with you, just as I pleaded for many, so he pleaded for Appius Claudius a little before his death.

You see, then, how we have come to you, the orator, Brutus, with so many orators interposed between our beginning of speaking and yours; of whom, since in this discourse of ours I have resolved to name none of those who were living — lest you should too curiously draw out from me what I judged of each — I shall name those who are now dead." Then Brutus said, "That is not the reason which you give, why you are unwilling to say anything about those who are living." "What, then," I said, "is it?" "I think," he said, "that you fear lest this discourse of yours should leak out through us, and lest those whom you have passed over should be angry with you." "What?" I said; "will you not be able to keep silent?" "We indeed most easily," he said; "but yet I think you prefer to keep silent yourself rather than to try our silence."

Then I said, "I will speak to you truly, Brutus. I did not think that in this discourse I should come down as far as this age; but the order of the ages so drew the discourse that I have now arrived even at the younger men." "Interpose, then," he said, "any you think fit; then let us return to you and to Hortensius." "Nay rather," I said, "to Hortensius; about myself others shall speak, if any wish." "By no means," he said. "For although you have easily held me by all your discourse, yet it seems to me longer because I am eager to hear about you; and not so much about the virtues of your speaking, which are most known both to all and certainly to me, as because I am eager to learn your steps and, as it were, your progress in speaking."

"It shall be done as you wish," I said, "since you wish me to be the proclaimer not of my talent but of my labour. But I will interpose, as you please, others, and will begin with Marcus Crassus, who was the equal of Hortensius.

He, then, moderately furnished with learning, and even more narrowly by nature, by labour and industry and because he brought to bear, for obtaining causes, care too and influence, was for some years among the leading advocates. In his oratory the Latin was good, the words not mean, the matter arranged diligently, no flower however nor any light, great straining of the spirit, little of the voice, everything spoken almost in like fashion and in one manner. For his equal and enemy Gaius Fimbria could not display himself so long; who, saying everything in a loud voice with a certain hurried rush of really good words, yet so raved that you would wonder that the people were doing other things, so that there was a place for a madman among the eloquent. Gnaeus Lentulus, however, by his delivery made a much greater impression of speaking than was the faculty in him; who, although he was neither very acute, although both from his face and from his expression he seemed so, nor abounding in words, although he deceived in this very thing — so by his pauses, exclamations, sweet and melodious voice, and admirable handling, he laughed, he grew warm in pleading, that the things which were lacking were not missed. So, as Curio held the place of an orator by some copiousness of words, with no other good: so Lentulus concealed the middling quality of his other oratorical virtues by delivery, in which he was excellent. And not much otherwise Publius Lentulus, whose slowness both of thinking and of speaking was covered by the dignity of his form, the movement of his body full of both art and grace, and the sweetness and greatness of his voice. So in this man there was nothing besides delivery, the rest even less than in the former.

Marcus Piso, whatever he had, he had from training, and most of all of those who lived before, he was educated in Greek learning. He had from nature a certain kind of keenness, which he had also polished by art, which was cunning and skilful in faulting words, but often peevish, sometimes frigid, at times even witty. He did not endure the labour of the forum, as a kind of race, very long, because he was both weak in body and did not bear the ineptitudes and follies of men, which must be swallowed by us, and spat them out rather angrily, whether peevishly, as was thought, or with an honest and free disdain. He, after he had flourished sufficiently as a young man, began afterwards to be held of less account. Then from the trial of the Vestals he gained great praise, and from that time, as if recalled into the race, he held his place as long as he could bear the labour; afterwards, as much as he took from his zeal, so much he lost of his glory.

Publius Murena, of middling talent, but of great zeal for ancient things, both fond of letters and not unskilled, was of much industry and great labour. Gaius Censorinus, learned enough in Greek letters, unfolding readily what he had proposed, not ungraceful a pleader, but inactive and an enemy of the forum. Lucius Turius, of small talent but of much labour, spoke often, in whatever way he could; and so a few centuries were wanting to him for the consulship.

Gaius Macer always lacked authority, but was a most diligent advocate, well-nigh. If his life, his morals, his very expression had not overturned all the recommendation of his talent, his name among advocates would have been greater. His oratory was not abundant, yet not poor; not very shining, not plainly rough; his voice, gesture, and all his delivery without charm; but in finding and arranging matters a wonderful accuracy, so that I have not easily known a more diligent or greater in anyone — but such that you would call it sooner crafty than oratorical. He, although he was approved even in public causes, yet held a more illustrious place in private ones.

Then Gaius Piso, a 'stationary' orator and full of conversation, not at all slow in devising, but yet by his expression and dissimulation seemed much more acute than he was. For his equal Manius Glabrio, well trained by the diligence of his grandfather Scaevola, his own sluggish and negligent nature had retarded. Lucius Torquatus too was elegant in speaking, very prudent in judging, in his whole kind very urbane. My equal Gnaeus Pompeius, a man born for all the highest things, would have had a greater glory of speaking, had not the desire of greater glory drawn him away to the praises of war. He was ample enough in oratory, saw the matter prudently; his delivery had both in his voice a great splendour and in his movement the highest dignity.

Likewise our equal Decimus Silanus, your stepfather, had not much zeal indeed, but enough of keenness and oratory. Quintus Pompeius, son of Aulus, who was called Bithynicus, perhaps older than us by two years, of the highest zeal for learning and much erudition, of incredible labour and industry — which I can know: for he was joined with me and with Marcus Piso both in friendship and in studies and exercises. His delivery did not sufficiently commend his oratory; for in the latter there was copiousness enough, but in the former too little charm.

His equal was Publius Autronius, of a very keen and great voice but commendable in no other respect, and Lucius Octavius of Reate, who, when he was already pleading many causes, died a young man — yet he came to speaking more boldly than preparedly —; and Gaius Staienus, who had adopted himself and made an Aelius out of a Staienus, of a certain heated and petulant and furious kind of speaking; which, because it was pleasing to many and was approved, he would have ascended to honours, had he not, caught in a manifest crime, paid the penalties to the laws and the court.

At the same time were the brothers Gaius and Lucius Caepasius, who by much effort, obscure and sudden men, were quickly made quaestors, with a certain provincial and unpolished kind of speaking. Let us add to these too, lest we seem to have passed over anyone vocal, Gaius Cosconius Calidianus, who with no keenness yet exhibited to the people that copiousness of words, if he had any, with much running about and great clamour. The same did Quintus Arrius, who was, as it were, Marcus Crassus's understudy. He ought to be an example to all of how much, in this city, it avails to comply with the convenience of many and to serve the honour or the peril of many.

For by these things, born in the lowest station, having attained both honours and money and influence, he had come even into some number among advocates — without learning, without talent. But as unexercised boxers, even if, eager for the Olympic games, they can bear blows and strokes, yet often cannot bear the sun, so he, when he had now prosperously discharged every fortune and had taken up even great labours, did not bear, as it were a sun, the severity of that judicial year.

Then Atticus said, "You are drawing now from the dregs, and have been for a while, but I held my peace; this, however, I did not think — that you would come down even to the Staieni and Autronii." "I do not suppose," I said, "that you think me carried away by partiality, since it is of the dead; but, following the order, I necessarily run into a known and contemporary memory. But I wish this to be perceived: that, all having been sought out who dared to speak among the multitude, very few indeed were worthy of memory, and that those who had any name at all were not so very many. But let us return to our appointed discourse.

Titus Torquatus, son of Titus, both a learned man from the Rhodian school of Molon and by nature loose and ready enough for speaking — to whom, had life been granted, with bribery removed he would have been made consul — had more faculty for speaking than will. And so he did not satisfy his study, but in his duty he was wanting neither in the causes of his own connections nor in giving his senatorial opinion.

Marcus Pontidius too, our townsman, regularly pleaded many private causes, rolling out his words quite quickly and not dull in causes, or rather I would say more than not dull, but boiling over in speaking often too vehemently with bile and anger; so that he often strove in altercation not only with his adversary but even, what was wonderful, with the judge himself, whose soother the orator ought to be. Marcus Messalla, younger than us, by no means poor, but not too ornate in his kind of words; prudent, acute, a least incautious advocate, diligent in learning and arranging causes, of great labour, of much effort and of many causes.

The two Metelli too, Celer and Nepos, somewhat engaged in causes, neither without talent nor unlearned, had attained this popular kind of speaking. Gnaeus Lentulus Marcellinus, however, was never without speech and in his consulship seemed very eloquent, not slow in thoughts, not poor in words, of melodious voice, witty enough. Gaius Memmius, son of Lucius, perfect in letters, but Greek, quite fastidious of Latin ones, a pointed orator and sweet in words, but, fleeing the labour not only of speaking but even of thinking, took as much from his own faculty as he diminished of his industry.

At this point Brutus said, "How I could wish that it pleased you to speak to me about those orators too who are alive today; and, if less about others, yet about the two whom I know you are wont to praise, Caesar and Marcellus, I would hear no less gladly than I have heard about those who have been." "Why, pray?" I said; "do you wait to hear what I judge about those who are equally known to you and to me?" "Marcellus, by Hercules," he said, "is well enough known to me,

but Caesar too little; for the former I have often heard, while the latter, when I could now judge something, was away." "What, then, do you judge about him," I said, "whom you have often heard?" "What do you think," he said, "except that which you are about to have — one like yourself?" "Indeed," I said, "if it is so, I should wish him to please you as much as possible." "And so it is," he said, "and he pleases me vehemently; nor indeed without cause. For he both learned, and, the other studies laid aside, gave himself to this one thing alone, and exercised himself most keenly with daily rehearsals.

And so he both uses choice words and frequent thoughts, and by the splendour of his voice and the dignity of his movement what he says is made specious and brilliant, and everything is so at hand that I think no virtue of an orator is lacking to him; and he is most to be praised, who at this very time, so far as is permitted in this our common and, as it were, fatal evil, consoles himself both with the consciousness of an excellent mind and also with the exercise and renewal of learning. For I saw lately at Mytilene a man, and, as I said, I saw plainly a man. And so, as I had before seen him like you in speaking, so now indeed, furnished by that most learned man Cratippus, and, as I understood, most friendly to you, with every copiousness, I saw him much more like."

Here I said, "Although I gladly hear the praises of an excellent man and most friendly to us, yet I run into the memory of our common miseries, the forgetfulness of which I have sought by prolonging this very conversation. But about Caesar I am eager to hear what after all Atticus may judge." And he said, "You hold to yourself admirably, in being unwilling yourself to say anything about those who are now living; and by Hercules, if you had dealt with them as you have dealt with those who are already dead, so as to pass over no one, you would indeed have run into many Autronii and Staieni. Wherefore, whether you wished to escape this throng, or feared lest anyone might complain that he had either been passed over or not sufficiently praised, you could nevertheless have spoken about Caesar, especially since both your judgement of his talent is most well known, and his judgement of yours not obscure. But yet, Brutus," said Atticus, "about Caesar both I myself so judge, and I very often hear from this most keen assessor of this kind, that he speaks Latin most elegantly of well-nigh all the orators; and that not only by domestic usage, as a while ago we were hearing about the families of the Laelii and the Mucii — but although I believe that too was the case, yet, that the praise of speaking well might be perfected, he has attained it by much study of letters, and those recondite and choice, and by the highest zeal and diligence: who even amid the greatest occupations has written most carefully to you yourself," he said, looking at me, "on the method of speaking Latin, and in his first book has said that the choice of words is the source of eloquence, and has ascribed to this friend of ours" — who preferred that I should speak of him rather than that he should speak of himself — "a singular praise, my Brutus; for he wrote in these words, having addressed him by name: 'And if, that they might express their excellent thoughts, some have laboured with study and practice — of which copiousness you, as well-nigh the chief and the inventor, we ought to judge to have deserved well of the name and dignity of the Roman people — is to have known this easy and everyday speech to be reckoned as a thing left behind?'

Then Brutus said, "Amicably indeed, by Hercules, and magnificently I think you praised — whom he called not only the chief and inventor of copiousness, which was great praise, but also one who deserved well of the name and dignity of the Roman people. For in that one thing in which we were surpassed by conquered Greece, that has either been wrested from them or at least shared by us with them. This glory and testimony of Caesar," he said, "I prefer not indeed to your supplication, but to the triumphs of many." "And rightly, Brutus," I said; "provided only that this is a testimony of Caesar's judgement, not of his goodwill. For surely he has brought more dignity to this people, whoever he is, if indeed there is anyone, who has not only illuminated but even begotten in this city the copiousness of speaking, than those who stormed the strongholds of the Ligurians: from which there are, as you know, many triumphs.

But if we wish to hear the truth, setting aside those divine counsels by which the wisdom of generals has often established the safety of the state in war or in peace, a great orator far excels petty generals. 'But a general is of more use.' Who denies it? But yet — I do not fear that you will cry out against me; for this is a place for speaking freely what you feel — I would rather have one speech of Lucius Crassus for Manius Curius than two triumphs over strongholds. 'But it was of more importance to the commonwealth that a stronghold of the Ligurians should be taken than that the cause of Manius Curius should be well defended.'

I believe it; but to the Athenians too it was of more importance to have firm roofs in their dwellings than the most beautiful statue of Minerva in ivory; yet I would rather be Phidias than even the best carpenter. Wherefore it is not how much each man is of use, but how much each man is worth, that must be weighed; especially since few can paint or model excellently, but workmen and porters cannot be lacking. But proceed, Pomponius, about Caesar, and render what remains."

"You see," said he, "the very ground and, as it were, foundation of the orator, correct and Latin diction, the praise of which has been hitherto in the hands of those whose praise it was not of method or knowledge, but, as it were, of good habit. I pass over Gaius Laelius and Publius Scipio: that praise of that age was, as of innocence, so of speaking Latin — and yet not of all, for we see their contemporaries Caecilius and Pacuvius speaking badly — but almost all then who had neither lived outside this city nor had been infected by any domestic barbarism, spoke correctly. But this matter at least antiquity has made worse, both at Rome and in Greece. For there flowed together both to Athens and to this city many speaking corruptly from various places. The more must speech be purified, and method applied, as a touchstone, which cannot be changed, and the most perverse rule of habit not be used.

Titus Flamininus, who was consul with Quintus Metellus, we saw as boys: he was thought to speak good Latin, but he knew no letters. Catulus indeed was by no means unlearned, as was said by you a little before, but yet the sweetness of his voice and the smooth pronunciation of the letters had made the fame of speaking well. Cotta, who by broadening the letters very much had drawn himself away from the likeness of Greek diction, and sounded the opposite of Catulus, something rather rural and plainly rather rustic, had by another, as it were uncultivated and woodland road arrived at the same praise. Sisenna, however, when he wished to be, as it were, a corrector of the customary speech, could not be deterred even by his accuser Gaius Rusius from using unusual words." "What, pray, is that?" said Brutus; "or who is that

Gaius Rusius?" And he said, "He was an accuser of old, on whose accusation, when Sisenna was defending Gaius Hirtilius, Sisenna said that certain of his charges were 'spit-aroundable.' Then Gaius Rusius said: 'I am circumvented, judges, unless you help me. What Sisenna means I do not know; I fear a trap. Spit-aroundable — what is this? What spit is, I know; aroundable I do not know.' Great was the laughter; but he, my friend, nevertheless thought that to speak unusually was to speak correctly.

Caesar, however, applying method, corrects faulty and corrupt habit by pure and incorrupt habit. And so when to this elegance of Latin words — which, even if you are not an orator and are a freeborn Roman citizen, is yet necessary — he joins those oratorical ornaments of speaking, then he seems, as it were, to set well-painted pictures in a good light. Since he has this special praise, in the common qualities I do not see to whom he ought to yield. He holds a certain splendid and least crafty method of speaking, magnificent and, in a certain way, noble in voice, movement, and even form."

Then Brutus said, "His speeches indeed I greatly approve. And I have read several, and also the commentaries which he wrote of his own deeds." "Greatly indeed to be approved," I said; "for they are bare, straight, and graceful, all ornament of oratory stripped away as a garment. But while he wished others to have material ready, from which those who wished to write history might take, he has perhaps done a favour to the inept, who will wish to crimp those with curling-irons: but sane men he has deterred from writing; for nothing is sweeter in history than pure and brilliant brevity. But let us, if you please, return to those who have departed from life.

Gaius Sicinius, then, the grandson by his daughter of that Quintus Pompeius who was censor, died of quaestorian rank; a commendable orator, nay even an approved one, from this school of Hermagoras, poor for adorning but ready for inventing. It gives sure methods and precepts of speaking, which, if they have less apparatus — for they are meagre — yet have order and certain roads that do not allow one to stray in speaking. Holding these, and coming prepared to causes, not poor in words, by that very equipment and discipline of speaking he had already come into the number of advocates.

There was also a learned man among the foremost, Gaius Visellius Varro, my cousin, who was joined in age with Sicinius. He, when after the curule aedileship he was judge of an inquiry, died; in whom I confess that the judgement of the crowd dissented from my judgement. For he was not sufficiently saleable to the people: a certain headlong oratory, obscure for this very reason that it was very acute, and rapid and blinded by speed; but I could not quickly name another apter in words nor more frequent in thoughts. Besides, perfect in letters, he held the discipline of civil law already handed down by his father Aculeo. There remain, of those who are dead, Lucius Torquatus, whom you would not so quickly have called a rhetor — although oratory was not lacking — as, as the Greeks say, a politikon. There were in him very many letters, and those not common, but certain deeper and more recondite; a divine memory, the highest both weight and elegance of words; and all these the weight and integrity of his life adorned. Me indeed the oratory of Triarius too, in that age full of lettered old age, greatly delighted. What severity in his face! what weight in his words! how nothing came out of his mouth unconsidered!

Then Brutus, moved by the mention of Torquatus and Triarius — for he had greatly loved each of them — said, "Indeed I, to omit the rest which are innumerable, when I think of those two, grieve that your perpetual authority on behalf of peace availed nothing! For the commonwealth would not have lost either those excellent men or many other outstanding citizens." "Let us be silent, Brutus," I said, "about those, lest we increase our grief. For both the recollection of things past is bitter, and the expectation of things to come more bitter. And so let us cease to mourn, and only proclaim how much each man could do by speaking, since that is what we seek.

There are also among those who fell in the same war, Marcus Bibulus, who both wrote carefully, although he was especially no orator, and conducted many things steadfastly; Appius Claudius, your father-in-law, my colleague and friend: he was now both studious enough and a very learned and even practised orator, and well skilled both in augural law and in all public law and in our antiquity. Lucius Domitius spoke indeed with no art, but yet in Latin and with much freedom.

There were besides two Lentuli of consular rank, of whom that Publius, the avenger of our wrongs, the author of our safety, whatever he had, however much it was, all that he had from training; the instruments of nature were lacking; but there was so great a splendour of mind and so great a greatness that he did not hesitate to claim for himself all the things that belong to illustrious men, and obtained them with every dignity. Lucius Lentulus, however, was a strong enough orator, if only an orator, but did not bear the labour of thinking; his voice melodious, his words not rough indeed, so that his oratory was full of spirit and terror; you would perhaps seek something better in the courts, but in public affairs you would judge that what there was, was enough.

Nor indeed is Titus Postumius to be despised in speaking; in public affairs indeed he was no less vehement an orator than a warrior, unbridled and too keen, but he had well learned the laws and institutions of public law."

At this point Atticus said, "I should think you ambitious, if, as you said, those whom you have now for a long time been collecting were living. For you mention all who ever dared to speak standing up, so that you seem to me unwittingly to have passed over Marcus Servilius."

"I am not ignorant of this, Pomponius," I said, "that there were many who had never uttered a word in public, although they could speak somewhat better than these orators whom I collect; but by mentioning these I attain this also, that you may understand, first, out of all the number, how not many dared to speak, and then, out of these very men, how few were worthy of praise.

And so I shall not omit even these Roman knights, our friends, who lately died: Publius Cominius of Spoletium, on whose accusation I defended Gaius Cornelius, in whom there was both a composed and a keen and ready kind of speaking; Titus Accius of Pisaurum, to whose accusation I answered for Aulus Cluentius, who both spoke carefully and copiously enough, and was besides learned in the precepts of Hermagoras, by which, although not very rich ornaments of speaking, yet, as javelins fitted with thongs for the light-armed, so certain arguments fitted and ready are handed down for the several kinds of causes.

And of greater zeal or industry I have known no one, although not even in talent could I easily say who surpassed Gaius Piso, my son-in-law. No time was ever free to him either from forensic pleading or from rehearsal at home or from writing or from thinking. And so he made such great progress that he seemed to fly rather than to run; and there was both an elegant choice of words and a fitting and, as it were, rounded construction; and while many and firm arguments were thought out by him for proving, there were besides neat and acute thoughts; and his gesture by nature so graceful that even art, which there was not, and a certain movement from training, seemed to come to it. I fear lest I may seem from love to say more than there was in him; which is not so; for other and greater things can be said about him. For neither in self-control nor in piety nor in any kind of virtue do I think anyone of the same age to be compared with him.

Nor indeed do I think Marcus Caelius is to be passed over, whatever his fortune or his mind was at the end; who, as long as he obeyed my authority, was such a tribune of the commons that no one stood more steadfastly against the popular and turbulent madness of abandoned citizens, on behalf of the senate and the cause of the good. His somewhat old-fashioned style of pleading was nevertheless commended much both by splendid and grand oratory and likewise among the foremost witty and very urbane. Some of his harangues were weighty, his accusations keen — three, and all undertaken from a contest of public affairs; his defences, although those things which I mentioned were better in him, were yet not to be despised and quite tolerable. He, when with the highest goodwill of the good he had been made curule aedile, somehow at my departure departed from himself and fell, after he began to imitate those whom he himself had overthrown. But about
