Marcus Calidius let us say something, who was not one orator out of many, but rather among many was almost singular: so did a soft and translucent oratory clothe his recondite and choice thoughts. Nothing so tender as that grouping of his words, nothing so flexible, nothing that was more moulded at his own will, so that it was in the power of no orator equally: which first was so pure that nothing more limpid, so freely it flowed that nowhere did it stick; you would see no word except set in its place and, as it were, constructed in a mosaic inlay, as Lucilius says; nor indeed any word either harsh or unusual or low or drawn out too far; and not the words proper to things, but most of them transferred, yet so that you would say that they had not rushed into another's place but had migrated into their own; nor indeed were these loose or flowing apart, but bound up by rhythm, not openly nor always in the same way but variously and dissemblingly rounded off.

There were too both of words and of thoughts those lights which the Greeks call schemata, by which, as by ornaments in adornment, his whole oratory was distinguished. And that 'point at issue,' which is included in many places in the formulae of the jurisconsults, he saw where it lay.

There was added an order of matters full of art, a free delivery, and a whole kind of speaking placid and sound. And if it is best to speak agreeably, there is nothing that you should think better than this to be sought. But since it was said by us a little before that there seem to be three things which an orator ought to accomplish — to instruct, to delight, to move — two he held in the highest degree, both to illustrate the matter by argument and to bind the minds of those who heard with pleasure; that third praise was lacking, by which he should thoroughly move and rouse minds, which we said had the most power; nor was there any force or straining: whether from design, because he judged that those whose oratory was loftier and delivery more ardent were raving and revelling, or because he was not so made by nature, or because he was not accustomed, or because he did not know how. This one thing was absent in him — if it had no usefulness; if it was needed, it was lacking.

Nay more, I remember that, when in his accusation he had charged Quintus Gallius with having prepared poison for him, and that this had been detected by him, and said that he was bringing forward handwritings, depositions, informations, examinations, the matter manifest, and had argued about that charge carefully and choicely, I, in answering, when I had argued as much as the matter bore, set this very thing also as an argument — that he, when he said that he had discovered the destruction of his own life, the proofs of his death, manifestly, and held them in his hand, had pleaded so loosely, so gently, so yawningly: 'Would you, Marcus Calidius,

unless you were inventing this, plead in this way? — especially since with that eloquence of yours you are wont most keenly to defend the perils of other men, would you neglect your own? Where is the grief? where the ardour of mind, which is wont to draw out cries and complaints even from the talents of infants? No disturbance of mind, none of body, no striking of the brow, none of the thigh; not even, what is the least thing, a stamping of the foot. And so so far was it from your inflaming our minds, that at that point we could scarcely keep from sleep.' So we used the soundness or the fault of a supreme orator as an argument to dissolve the charge."

Then Brutus said, "And do we doubt whether that was soundness or a fault? For who would not confess that, since of all the praises of the orator that is by far the greatest — to inflame the minds of the hearers and to bend them in whatever way the matter demands — he who lacked this virtue was lacking in that which was the greatest?" "Let it be so indeed," I said; "but let us return to him who now alone remains, Hortensius, and then we shall say a few words about ourselves, since that too, Brutus, you ask. Although mention is to be made, as at least it seems to me, of two young men, who, had they lived longer, would have attained a great praise of eloquence."

"You mean," said Brutus, "Gaius Curio and Gaius Licinius Calvus." "You judge rightly," I said; "of whom the one rolled out so easily and fluently thoughts at times acute enough, frequent at least certainly, that nothing could be more ornate, nothing readier. And this man, too little trained by teachers, had an admirable nature for speaking; his industry I have not tried, his zeal certainly there was. Who, had he been willing to hear me, as he had begun, would have preferred to attain honours rather than power." "What, pray," he said, "is that? and how do you distinguish it?" "In this way," I said.

"Since honour is the reward of virtue conferred upon someone by the judgement and zeal of the citizens, he who has attained it by their opinions, by their votes, seems to me both honourable and honoured. But he who by some chance has obtained command even against the will of his fellow citizens, as that man desired, has, I think, attained the name of honour, not honour. Which, had he been willing to hear, he would have come, with the greatest favour and glory, to the highest greatness, ascending by the steps of the magistracies, as his father had done, as the other more illustrious men. These very things I think I often discussed with Publius Crassus, son of Marcus, too, when at the outset of his age he had betaken himself to my friendship, when I vehemently exhorted him to consider that the straightest road of praise was that which his ancestors had left worn for him.

For he was both most excellently trained and also perfectly and plainly learned, and there was in him both a talent keen enough and a not inelegant copiousness of oratory; and besides he seemed weighty without arrogance and modest without sloth. But this man too a certain tide of glory unusual for young men absorbed; who, because he had done good service as a soldier to a general, desired at once to be a general himself — an office to which the custom of our ancestors left a fixed age, an uncertain lot. So by his most grievous fall, while he wished to be like Cyrus and Alexander, who had run through their own course, he was found most unlike Lucius Crassus and many Crassi.

But let us return to Calvus — for he was the one set before us; who was an orator both more learned in letters than Curio, and also brought a certain more careful and more choice kind of speaking; which, although he handled it knowingly and elegantly, yet, too much inquiring into himself and observing himself and fearing lest he should gather something faulty, he lost even the true blood. And so his oratory, attenuated by excessive scruple, was brilliant to the learned and to attentive hearers, but by the multitude and by the forum, for which eloquence was born, was swallowed up.

Then Brutus said, "Our Calvus wished to be called an Attic orator: thence was that meagreness which he attained of set purpose." "He said so," I said; "but he both erred himself and forced others too to err. For if anyone thinks that those who speak neither ineptly nor odiously nor affectedly speak in the Attic manner, he rightly approves no one except an Attic. For he hates insipidity and extravagance, as a kind of madness of oratory, but approves soundness and integrity, as a kind of scruple and modesty of the orator. This ought to be the same opinion of all orators.

But if he places meagreness and dryness and poverty, provided only it be polished, provided urbane, provided elegant, in the Attic kind, this is right only so far; but because among the Attics some are better than others, let him beware lest he be ignorant of the degrees and the differences and the force and the variety of the Attics. 'I wish to imitate the Attics,' he says. Which? for there is not one kind. For what is so unlike as Demosthenes and Lysias? as the same and Hyperides? as of all these Aeschines? Whom, then, do you imitate? If someone: did the rest, then, not speak in the Attic manner? if all: how can you, when they themselves are most unlike one another? In which I ask this too — whether that Demetrius of Phalerum spoke in the Attic manner. To me indeed Athens herself seems to breathe from his speeches. But he is more florid, so to speak, than Hyperides, than Lysias: a certain nature or a will of speaking thus there was.

And indeed there were two at the same time unlike each other, but Attic nevertheless; of whom Charisius was of many speeches, which he wrote for others, when he seemed to desire to imitate Lysias; Demochares, however, who was the son of Demosthenes's sister, both wrote some speeches and wrote out the history of those things which were done at Athens in his own age, not so much in a historical as in an oratorical kind. And Hegesias wishes to be like Charisius, and so thinks himself Attic that he thinks those true Attics almost rustic in comparison with himself.

But what is so broken, so minced, so puerile in that very neatness which nevertheless he attains? 'We wish to be like the Attics.' Excellent; are these, then, Attic orators? 'Who can deny it? These we imitate.' How — they who are both unlike one another and unlike others? 'We imitate Thucydides,' he says. Excellent, if you think of writing history, not if of pleading causes. For Thucydides was a genuine and even grand narrator of deeds; this forensic, contentious, judicial kind he did not handle. But the speeches which he interposed — for there are many — those I am wont to praise; to imitate I could not, if I wished, nor would I perhaps, if I could. As if someone delights in Falernian wine, but neither so new that he would wish it born in the last consulship, nor again so old that he would seek a consul Opimius or Anicius — 'and yet these vintages are the best,' I believe; but excessive age has not that sweetness which we seek, nor is it now really tolerable —

would he, then, who feels this, if he wished to drink, think he must draw for himself from the vat? By no means; but let him follow a certain age. So I should advise those men that both this new oratory, as it were hot from the must and the vat, is to be fled, and that excellent one of Thucydides, too old, like the Anician vintage, is not to be pursued. For Thucydides himself, had he lived later, would have been much riper and milder. 'Let us, then, imitate Demosthenes.' O good gods; what else, I ask, do we do, or what else do we wish? But we do not attain it. For these our Attics, forsooth, attain what they wish.

They do not even understand this — not only that it is so recorded, but that it was necessarily so, that, when Demosthenes was about to speak, gatherings for the sake of hearing took place from all Greece. But when these Attics speak, they are left not only by the bystanders — which is itself pitiable — but even by their own supporters. Wherefore if to speak narrowly and meagrely is the mark of the Attics, let them indeed be Attic; but let them come into the comitium, let them speak before a standing judge: the benches demand a grander and fuller voice.

I wish this to fall to the orator's lot — that when it has been heard that he is about to speak, a place on the benches is taken, the tribunal is filled, the clerks are obliging in giving and yielding a place, the throng manifold, the judge erect; when he who is about to speak rises, silence is signified by the throng, then frequent assents, many expressions of admiration; laughter when he wishes, weeping when he wishes: so that he who sees these things from afar, even if he does not know what is being done, understands nevertheless that he is pleasing, and that a Roscius is on the stage. He to whose lot these things fall, know that he speaks in the Attic manner, as we hear of Pericles, as of Hyperides, as of Aeschines, and indeed of Demosthenes himself most of all.

But if they approve an acute, prudent, and likewise genuine and solid and dried-up kind of oratory, and do not use that weightier oratorical ornament, and wish this to be the property of the Attics, they praise rightly. For in an art so great and so varied there is a place even for this minute subtlety. So it will come about that not all who speak in the Attic manner speak likewise well, but that all who speak well speak likewise in the Attic manner too. But let us return again to Hortensius."

"Certainly indeed," said Brutus; "although that digression of yours from the proposed discourse was most pleasant to me." Then Atticus said, "Several times I have attempted to, but I was unwilling to interrupt. Now, since your discourse seems already to look toward concluding, I shall say, I think, what I feel." "Do indeed, Titus," I said. Then he said, "I think that irony which they say was in Socrates, which he uses in the books of Plato and Xenophon and Aeschines, witty and elegant. For it is the mark both of a least inept man and likewise of a witty one, when there is a dispute about wisdom, to take this away from himself, to ascribe it, mocking, to those who arrogate it to themselves — as in Plato Socrates extols to heaven with praises Protagoras, Hippias, Prodicus, Gorgias, and the rest, but feigns himself ignorant and rude in all things. This somehow becomes him, nor do I agree with Epicurus, who censures it. But in history, which you have used in your whole discourse, when you set forth what kind of orator each man was, see, pray," he said, "lest irony be as much to be censured as in giving testimony." "To what end is that?" I said; "for I do not understand.

Because, first," he said, "you praised certain orators in such a way that you could lead the inexperienced into error. For my part, in some cases I could scarcely keep from laughing, when you compared to the Attic Lysias our Cato — a great man, by Hercules, or rather a supreme and singular man — no one will say otherwise — but an orator? but even like Lysias? than whom nothing can be more polished. A pretty irony, if we were jesting; but if we are asserting, see lest scruple be as much to be applied by us as if we were giving testimony.

For I approve your Cato as a citizen, as a senator, as a general, as a man, in short, excellent both in prudence and diligence and in every virtue; his speeches I greatly praise for those times — for they signify a certain form of talent, but very unpolished and plainly rude — but when you said that his Origins were crammed with all the praises of an orator, and compared Cato with Philistus and Thucydides, did you think you would approve that to Brutus or to me? For to those whom not even any of the Greeks can imitate, you compare a man of Tusculum not yet even suspecting what it was to speak copiously and ornately.

You praise Galba. If as the leading man of that age, I assent — for so we have been told —; but if as an orator, produce, pray, his speeches — for there are some — and say that this Brutus, whom you love more than yourself, you wish to speak in that manner. You approve the speeches of Lepidus — here, Paulus, I assent to you, provided you praise them as ancient; which likewise I say of Africanus, of Laelius, than whose oratory you say nothing can be made sweeter, and you add too something or other more solemn. You catch us with the name of a supreme man and with most true praises of a most elegant life. Remove these: lest that sweet oratory be so mean that no one would wish to look at it.

I know that Carbo was held among the supreme orators; but, as in other things so in speaking, what is now the best, that, of whatever kind it is, is wont to be praised. I say the same of the Gracchi, although about them those things have been said by you to which I assent. I pass over the rest; I come to those in whom you think eloquence now perfected, whom I have heard, without dispute great orators, Crassus and Antonius. To their praises I wholly assent to you, but yet not in that manner: as Lysippus said that the Doryphorus of Polyclitus was his master, so you say that the advocacy of the Servilian law was your mistress; this is genuine irony. Why I think so I shall not say, lest you think I am flattering you.

I pass over, then, what you said about these very men, what about Cotta, what about Sulpicius, what just now about Caelius. For these were certainly orators; but how great and of what kind, you may see for yourself. For that I care less about — that you have heaped together all the workmen; so that some seem to me to have wished to die, in order to be entered by you in the number of orators." When he had said this: "You have set in motion the beginning of a long discourse, Atticus," I said, "and have stirred a matter worthy of a new disputation, which let us put off to another time.

For the books both of others and especially of Cato are to be turned over. You will understand that nothing was lacking to his outlines except the bloom and colour of those pigments which had not yet been discovered. For about the oratory of Crassus I judge thus, that he himself perhaps could have written better, but no one else, as I think. For in this you would not take me to be an ironist, because I have said that that speech was my mistress. For although you yourself seem to judge better of that faculty, if any, which we now have, yet as young men we had nothing in the Latins rather to imitate.

But that more were named by me, this pertained to it, as I said a little before, that I wished it to be understood, in that which all were most eager for, how few came out worthy of the name. Wherefore I would not have myself thought an ironist, not even if Africanus was one, as Gaius Fannius says in his history." "As you will," said Atticus. "For I did not think it foreign to you, what had been both in Africanus and in Socrates."

Then Brutus said, "About that later; but you," he said, looking at me, "will you set forth for us the old speeches?" "Indeed, Brutus," I said; "but at my place at Cumae or at Tusculum at some time, if only it shall be permitted, since in each place we are neighbours. But now let us return to that from which we digressed.

Hortensius, then, when as a quite young man he had begun to speak in the forum, was quickly taken up for greater causes: and although he had fallen upon the age of Cotta and Sulpicius, who were ten years older, with Crassus and Antonius then excelling, then Philippus, afterwards Julius, with these very men his glory of speaking was compared. First, a memory so great as I think I have known in no one, that what he had rehearsed with himself, that he rendered without writing in the same words in which he had thought it. This aid he used, so great, in such a way that he remembered both his own things rehearsed and written, and, with no one prompting, all that all his adversaries had said.

And he burned with eagerness so that in no one have I ever seen a more flaming zeal. For he allowed no day to pass without either speaking in the forum or rehearsing outside the forum. Very often, however, he did both on the same day. And he had brought a by no means common kind of speaking; two things indeed which no one else: divisions of the matters about which he was to speak, and recapitulations, mindful both of what had been said against him and of what he himself had said.

He was elegant in the splendour of his words, apt in arrangement, copious in faculty; and these he had attained both by the highest talent and by the greatest exercises. He embraced the matter from memory, divided it acutely, and passed over almost nothing that was in the cause either for confirming or for refuting. His voice melodious and sweet, his movement and gesture had even more art than was enough for an orator. While he, then, was flourishing, Crassus died, Cotta was driven out, the courts were interrupted by the war, and we came into the forum.

Hortensius in the war was in the first year a soldier, in the second a military tribune; Sulpicius a lieutenant; Marcus Antonius too was away; the courts were exercised by the one Varian law, the rest interrupted on account of the war; at which I was frequently present, although the orators pleaded for themselves not indeed leading ones, Lucius Memmius and Quintus Pompeius, but orators nevertheless, with the eloquent witness, at any rate, Philippus, in whose testimony the straining had both the force and the copiousness of an accuser.

The rest who were then counted leading men were in magistracies and were heard by us almost daily in the assemblies. For the tribune of the commons then was Gaius Curio, although he indeed was silent, as he had once been left by an entire assembly; Quintus Metellus Celer, not indeed an orator, but yet not without speech; but eloquent were Quintus Varius, Gaius Carbo, Gnaeus Pomponius, and these indeed dwelt on the Rostra; Gaius Julius too, the curule aedile, held almost daily carefully prepared assemblies. But me, most eager to hear, the first grief struck, when Cotta was expelled. Frequently hearing the rest, I was held by a most keen zeal, and daily both writing and reading and rehearsing I was not content with oratorical exercises alone. Now in the following year Quintus Varius, condemned by his own law, had departed;

but I gave much labour to the study of civil law with Quintus Scaevola, son of Quintus, who, although he gave himself to no one for teaching, yet, by answering those who consulted him, taught those eager to hear. And the year next to this was that of the consuls Sulla and Pompeius. Then we came thoroughly to know the whole kind of speaking of Publius Sulpicius, haranguing daily in his tribunate; and at the same time, when Philo, the head of the Academy, with the optimates of the Athenians, had fled from home in the Mithridatic war and had come to Rome, I gave myself wholly to him, roused by a certain admirable zeal for philosophy, in which I dwelt the more attentively — although the variety and great magnitude of the matters themselves held me with the highest delight — because the method of the courts seemed now to have been taken away for ever.

Sulpicius had fallen that year, and in the next three orators of three ages had been most cruelly killed, Quintus Catulus, Marcus Antonius, Gaius Julius. In the same year too at Rome we gave our attention to Molon of Rhodes, both a supreme pleader of causes and a teacher. These things, although they seem to be foreign to the proposed discourse, are nevertheless brought forward by me for this reason — that you may be able to discern our course, since you wished it, Brutus — for to Atticus these things are known — and to see how, in the race, we followed Quintus Hortensius in his very footsteps. For nearly three years the city was without arms, but by the death or departure or flight of the orators — for the young men Marcus Crassus and the two Lentuli were also away — Hortensius pleaded the first parts in causes; Antistius was more and more approved daily, Piso spoke often, Pomponius less often, Carbo rarely, Philippus once or twice. But I at all this time, nights and days, was engaged in the meditation of all the disciplines.

I was with the Stoic Diodotus, who, when he had dwelt with me and lived with me, lately died in my house. By him I was exercised, both in other things and most eagerly in dialectic, which is to be thought, as it were, a contracted and compressed eloquence; without which even you, Brutus, have judged that you could not attain that genuine eloquence, which they think to be dialectic dilated. To this teacher and to his various and many arts I was nevertheless so devoted that no day was free from oratorical exercises.

I rehearsed, declaiming — for so they now speak — often with Marcus Piso and with Quintus Pompeius or with someone daily, and I did this much in Latin too, but more often in Greek, either because Greek oratory, supplying more ornaments, brought a habit of speaking similarly in Latin, or because by the supreme Greek teachers, unless I spoke Greek, I could neither be corrected nor taught.

Meanwhile there was tumult in the recovery of the commonwealth and the cruel death of the three orators Scaevola, Carbo, Antistius, the return of Cotta, Curio, Crassus, the Lentuli, Pompeius, the laws and courts established, the commonwealth recovered; but from the number of orators Pomponius, Censorinus, Murena were taken away. Then first we began to come to causes both private and public, not in order to learn in the forum, which most did, but in order that, as much as we could accomplish, we might come into the forum already learned.

At the same time we gave our attention to Molon; for, in the dictatorship of Sulla, he had come as a lieutenant to the senate about the rewards of the Rhodians. And so our first public cause, pleaded for Sextus Roscius, had so much of commendation that there was none which did not seem worthy of our advocacy. Then thereafter many, which we brought diligently elaborated and, as it were, worked out by lamplight.

Now, since you seem to wish to know me not by some mole or rattle but by the whole body, I shall embrace some things too which may perhaps seem less necessary. There was at that time in me the highest slenderness and weakness of body, a long and thin neck: which habit and which figure are thought not to be far from peril of life, if labour and a great straining of the sides is added. And this moved the more those to whom I was dear, because I said everything without remission, without variety, with the highest force of voice and straining of the whole body.

And so, when both friends and physicians urged me to cease pleading causes, I thought that any peril whatever was rather to be undergone than that I should depart from the hoped-for glory of speaking. But since I judged that by remission and moderation of the voice and by changing the kind of speaking I could both avoid the peril and speak more temperately, that I might change my habit of speaking was the cause of my setting out into Asia. And so, when I had been engaged in causes for two years and my name was now celebrated in the forum, I set out from Rome.

When I had come to Athens, I was six months with Antiochus, the most noble and most prudent philosopher of the Old Academy, and the study of philosophy, never interrupted and cultivated from earliest youth and always increased, I renewed again with this supreme author and teacher. At the same time, however, at Athens with Demetrius the Syrian, an old and not ignoble teacher of speaking, I was wont to be exercised eagerly. Afterwards all Asia was traversed by me, with the supreme orators indeed, with whom I was exercised, they themselves being willing; of whom the chief was Menippus of Stratonicea, in my judgement in all Asia in those times the most eloquent; and, if to have nothing of the troubles and ineptitudes of the Attics is to be Attic, this orator can rightly be numbered among them.

But most constantly with me was Dionysius of Magnesia; there was also Aeschylus of Cnidos, and Xenocles of Adramyttium. These were then counted the chief of the rhetors in Asia. Not content with whom, I came to Rhodes and applied myself to the same Molon whom I had heard at Rome, both an outstanding pleader in real causes and a writer, and most prudent in marking and noting faults and in training and teaching. He gave his attention, if only he could attain it, to repressing us, too redundant and overflowing with a certain juvenile licence and unrestraint of speaking, and to confining us, as it were flowing beyond our banks. So I returned, two years later, not only more practised but almost changed. For both the excessive straining of the voice had subsided and the oratory had, as it were, boiled down, and strength had come to the sides and a moderate habit to the body.

Two orators then excelled who might rouse me with a desire of imitating them, Cotta and Hortensius; of whom the one was relaxed and gentle and embracing the thought loosely and easily in proper words, the other ornate, keen, and not such as you, Brutus, knew him, already fading, but more excitable in his kind of words and delivery. And so I judged that my business was rather with Hortensius, both because in ardour of speaking I was nearer and in age more closely joined. For indeed I had seen, in the same causes — as for Marcus Canuleius, for the consular Gnaeus Dolabella — that, although Cotta had been employed as the leading man, yet Hortensius pleaded the first parts. For a keen orator, kindled and active and melodious, the concourse of men and the noise of the forum demands.

For one year, then, when we had returned from Asia, we pleaded noble causes, while I was seeking the quaestorship, Cotta the consulship, Hortensius the aedileship. Meanwhile the Sicilian year received me as quaestor, Cotta set out from his consulship into Gaul, Hortensius both was and was held the leading man. But when, a year later, I had returned from Sicily, that thing in me, whatever it was, now seemed to be perfected and to have a certain maturity of its own. I seem to say too much about myself, especially as I am myself the one; but the purpose of all this discourse is not that you should perceive my talent and eloquence, from which I am far, but my labour and industry.

When, then, I had been engaged for nearly five years in very many causes and among the leading advocates, then in my Sicilian advocacy I came into the greatest contest, as aedile-elect with the consul-elect Hortensius. But since all this discourse of ours requires not only an enumeration of orators but also certain precepts, what is, as it were, to be marked and noted in Hortensius may be briefly said.

For he, after his consulship — I believe because he saw that none of the consulars was to be compared with him, and neglected those who had not been consuls — relaxed that highest zeal of his with which from a boy he had been kindled, and in the abundance of all things wished to live more happily, as he himself thought, certainly more relaxedly. The first and second and third year had taken away just so much, as it were, from the colour of an old picture, as not any one of the people, but a learned and understanding assessor could perceive. Proceeding further, however, as in the other parts of eloquence, so most of all sticking in the swiftness and continuation of words, he seemed to become daily more unlike himself.

But we did not cease, both with every kind of exercise and most of all with the pen, to increase that thing of ours, whatever it was, however much it was. And, to omit many things in this interval and in these years after the aedileship, I was made both praetor first and, with incredible goodwill of the people, consul. For both on account of my assiduity in causes and my industry, and on account of a more choice and least common kind of oratory, I had turned the minds of men to me by the novelty of my speaking.

I shall say nothing about myself: I shall speak of the rest, of whom there was no one who seemed to have studied letters, in which the source of perfect eloquence is contained, more choicely than the common run of men; no one who had embraced philosophy, the mother of all well-done deeds and well-said words; no one who had learned the civil law, a thing most necessary for private causes and for the prudence of the orator; no one who held the memory of Roman affairs, from which, if ever there were need, he might raise from the dead the most wealthy witnesses; no one who, briefly and pointedly, his adversary mocked, could relax the minds of the judges and lead them for a while from severity to mirth and laughter; no one who could dilate, and lead the oratory from a proper and definite discussion of a person and a time to a common question of the whole kind; no one who, for the sake of delighting, could digress for a little from the cause; no one who could lead the judge greatly to anger, no one who could lead him to weeping; no one who could impel his mind — which alone is most especially the property of the orator — in whatever direction the matter demanded.

And so, when Hortensius had now almost faded away, and I had been made consul in my own year, but in the sixth after he was consul, he began to recall himself to industry, lest, when we were equal in honour, I should seem to be superior in some respect. So for twelve years after my consulship we were engaged most closely together in the greatest causes, while I preferred him to myself, and he me to himself; and my consulship, which at first had lightly grazed him, the same had joined us by the praise of my deeds, which he admired.

But the practice of each of us was most especially perceived a little before this pursuit of ours, terrified by arms, Brutus, suddenly fell silent and grew dumb: when, under the Pompeian law with three hours given for speaking, we came new every day to causes most like one another, or rather the very same. At which causes you too, Brutus, were present, and pleaded several both with us and alone, so that Hortensius, though he did not live long enough, yet completed this course: he began to plead causes sixteen years before you were born; the same man, in his sixty-fourth year, very few days before his death, together with you defended your father-in-law Appius. But what the kind of speaking was in each, the speeches of each will show even to our posterity.

But if we ask why Hortensius flourished more in speaking as a young man than as an older one, we shall find two most true causes. The first, that his kind of oratory was Asiatic, more granted to youth than to old age. Now there are two kinds of Asiatic diction: one sententious and pointed, with thoughts not so much weighty and severe as neat and graceful, such as Timaeus in history, but in speaking, when we were boys, Hierocles of Alabanda, and even more his brother Menecles, of both of whom the speeches are among the foremost praiseworthy in the Asiatic kind. The other kind is not so much crowded with thoughts as winged and impetuous in words, such as is now all Asia, and not only in the flow of oratory, but also in an embellished and witty kind of words, in which were Aeschylus of Cnidos and my contemporary Aeschines of Miletus. In these there was an admirable run of oratory, but the ornate neatness of thoughts there was not.

But these kinds of speaking, as I said, are fitter for young men; in old men they have no weight. And so Hortensius, flourishing in each kind, raised loud applause as a young man. For he had both that Meneclean zeal for frequent and graceful thoughts — in which, as in that Greek, so in him there were certain thoughts more graceful and sweet than either necessary or sometimes useful — and his oratory was both impetuous and vibrant and also careful and polished. These things were not approved by old men — I often saw Philippus both mocking and even growing angry and peevish — but young men admired, the multitude was moved. He was excellent in the judgement of the crowd and easily held the first place as a young man. For although that kind of speaking had too little of authority, yet it seemed suited to his age. And certainly, because both a certain form of talent shone out and a perfect exercise of words bound up in a compact grouping, he excited the highest admiration of men. But when now honours and that older authority required something weightier, he remained the same, and the same did not become him; and because he had let go his exercise and zeal, which in him had been most keen, that former neatness and frequency of thoughts remained, but it was not adorned with that dress of oratory with which he had been wont. This, perhaps, Brutus, pleased you less than it would have pleased, if you had been able to hear him flaming with zeal and flourishing in faculty."

Then Brutus said, "For my part I both see of what kind those things are which you say, and I always thought Hortensius a great orator, and most especially approved him speaking for Messalla, when you were away." "So they report," I said, "and his speech, written, as they say, in just as many words as he spoke, declares it. Therefore he flourished from the consulship of Crassus and Scaevola down to the consuls Paullus and Marcellus; we were in the same course from the dictatorship of Sulla to nearly the same consuls. So the voice of Quintus Hortensius was extinguished by his own fate, ours by the public fate.

"Make a better omen, pray," said Brutus. "Let it be indeed as you wish," I said, "and that not so much for my sake as for yours; but fortunate was his end, who did not see, when they happened, those things which he foresaw would come. For often between ourselves we bewailed the impending disasters, when we saw the causes of civil war shut up in the desires of private men, and the hope of peace shut out from the public counsel. But his own good fortune, which he always enjoyed, seems to have rescued him by death from those miseries which followed.

But we, Brutus, since after the death of Hortensius, that most illustrious orator, we have been left as the, as it were, guardians of orphaned eloquence, let us keep her at home, hedged about with a free protection, and let us repudiate these unknown and shameless suitors, and guard her as a grown maiden, chastely, and as far as we can keep her from the assault of lovers. For my part, although I grieve that I entered upon life a little too late, as it were upon a road, and, before the journey was completed, fell into this night of the commonwealth, yet I am sustained by that consolation which you, Brutus, applied to me in your most pleasant letter, in which you judged that I ought to be of brave spirit, because I had done those things which would speak of me even with me silent, and would live when I was dead; which, if all went rightly, by the safety of the commonwealth, but if otherwise, by its very destruction, would give testimony of my counsels concerning the commonwealth.

But looking on you, Brutus, I grieve — you, whose youth, as it rode, as it were, in a four-horse chariot through the midst of praises, the cross-blow of the commonwealth's wretched fortune has run athwart. This grief touches me, this care troubles me, and this man with me, the partner of the same love and judgement. We favour you, we desire that you may enjoy your virtue, we wish for you that commonwealth in which you may be able to renew and increase the memory of two most distinguished families. For yours was that forum, yours that course; you had come there, you alone, who had not only sharpened your tongue by the practice of speaking, but had also enriched eloquence itself with the equipment of weightier arts, and by those same arts had joined every glory of virtue with the highest praise of eloquence.

From you a twofold anxiety afflicts us — that you yourself are deprived of the commonwealth and it of you. Yet you, Brutus, although this untimely calamity of the state checks the course of your talent, hold yourself to your perennial studies, and accomplish that which you had now well-nigh, or rather plainly, accomplished — that you may rescue yourself from that throng of advocates which I have gathered into this discourse. For it does not befit you, adorned with the richest arts, which, since you could not draw them from home, you summoned from that city which has always been held the home of learning, to be numbered among the common crowd of advocates. For why did Pammenes, by far the most eloquent man of Greece, train you? why that old Academy and its heir Aristus, my host and friend, if indeed we are going to be like the greater part of orators?

Do we not see that scarcely in single ages have two praiseworthy orators stood forth? Galba was, among so many of his contemporaries, the one outstanding man, to whom, as we have been told, both the elder Cato yielded and those who were younger in those times — Lepidus afterwards, then Carbo; for the Gracchi in their harangues with a far easier and freer kind of speaking, although even to their age the praise of eloquence had not yet been perfected; Antonius, Crassus, after them Cotta, Sulpicius, Hortensius. I say no more, I only say this: if it had befallen me to be numbered among the many . . . if the running-about of the more opportune is laborious . . .
